# AGENTS.md

Rules for anyone changing this repository: AI coding agents and people. Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI and OpenCode all read this file. Do not add a `CLAUDE.md` at the repo root: by default, Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md` only when no `CLAUDE.md` exists in the working directory or above it ([Claude Code memory](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory)). The image's seeded `rootfs/etc/agentainer/home/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is a different file. [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) covers branches, CI and releases.

## What this repo is

Agentainer is one public container image that bundles four AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Antigravity CLI, OpenCode) and a shared toolset. It runs locally with Podman or Docker and in Kubernetes through ContainerSSH.

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `Containerfile`, `build/` | The image build and the scripts it runs |
| `versions.env` | Every pinned version, digest and checksum |
| `rootfs/` | Files copied into the image: the entrypoint and its steps, `agentainer-*` commands, seeded configs |
| `bin/agentainer` | The host launcher (POSIX sh) |
| `deploy/kubernetes/` | The Kubernetes example: StatefulSet, ContainerSSH, auth webhook |
| `scripts/` | Build, scheduled pin update, CI report scripts |
| `tests/` | Container tests (`NN-*.sh`), host tests (`host/`), unit tests (`unit/`), fixtures |
| `docs/` | User documentation |
| `.github/workflows/` | CI, release and the scheduled update |
| `Containerfile.kelos`, `rootfs-kelos/`, `tests/kelos/` | The Kelos variant image, its files and its tests ([docs/kelos.md](docs/kelos.md)). Its pins live in `Containerfile.kelos`, not `versions.env`. CI does not build or test it. |

`docs/private/` holds the maintainer's design notes, may be stale, and is ignored by git. Never commit anything under it.

## Commands

```sh
scripts/build.sh                            # build localhost/agentainer:dev
sh tests/run.sh [tests/NN-name.sh ...]      # container tests
sh tests/lint.sh                            # shellcheck, shfmt and Ruff
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests/unit
sh tests/14-unit-linux.sh                   # image Python and Linux-only unit modules
sh tests/host/test-launcher.sh
sh tests/host/test-build-script.sh
sh tests/host/test-fetch.sh
sh tests/host/test-manifests.sh
sh tests/host/test-launcher-integration.sh  # real engine, existing local image
sh tests/host/test-build-uid.sh             # slow: full build with --uid 1001 --gid 20
python3 tests/host/test-layer-repro.py      # slow: two clean tool builds, configured Buildx
python3 tests/host/test-healthcheck.py      # also invoked by tests/58-healthcheck.sh
python3 tests/host/test-language-tooling.py --image localhost/agentainer:dev  # slow, network
python3 tests/host/test-playwright-setup.py --image localhost/agentainer:dev  # slow, network
scripts/build.sh --variant kelos [--from IMAGE]                 # build localhost/agentainer-kelos:dev; network
IMAGE=localhost/agentainer-kelos:dev sh tests/kelos/test_image.sh
# Release verification arguments: docs/versions.md#verifying-a-release-before-use
# Optional terminal screenshots: tests/visual/README.md
```

Check each command's exit code directly. Piping into `tail` or `grep` hides a failure.

## Verify, never guess

- Every package name, version, install command, config path, file name, flag and URL must come from the tool's official docs, its official repository, or a command you ran. Cite the source next to the fact in docs and in commit or pull request text.
- If you cannot verify something, write "not verified" and ask the maintainer. If sources disagree, show both and let the maintainer choose.
- Check a CLI flag with `--help`, a man page or the tool's source before you use it.
- A recommendation is not a decision. Design changes need the maintainer's approval first.

## Public and generic

- The repo is public and MIT licensed. Anyone must be able to use it.
- Never commit internal information: hostnames, IP addresses, cluster names, registry names, domains or network details from anyone's own infrastructure. Use `example.com` and `203.0.113.0/24` in examples.
- Never put credentials in the image, in any layer, or in the repo. Credentials come in at run time through environment variables or the home volume.

## Pins and downloads

- Every pinned version, digest and checksum for the image lives in `versions.env`. Do not hardcode versions in the `Containerfile` or scripts. Exceptions: GitHub Actions and the actionlint image are pinned by SHA or digest in the workflow files, and the deploy image references (`CONTAINERSSH_IMAGE` and `WEBHOOK_PYTHON_IMAGE` in `deploy/kubernetes/*/deployment.yaml`, `FILEBROWSER_IMAGE` in `deploy/kubernetes/agentainer/statefulset.yaml`) repeat their `versions.env` pins (`bump_versions.py` rewrites them and `tests/host/test-manifests.sh` checks they match). The optional extras keep their dependency hashes in `rootfs/usr/local/share/agentainer/extras/<name>/package-lock.json`, and each `package.json` there repeats its `versions.env` pin (`bump_versions.py` rewrites both and `tests/host/test-extras-catalog.sh` checks they match).
- A new pin needs a resolver in `scripts/bump_versions.py`, unless the scheduled update must never change it (`SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`). Its key must match a pattern in `VALUE_PATTERNS` (most keys match by suffix, such as `_VERSION` or `_SHA256_ARM64`). The scheduled update refuses to write a value that matches no pattern.
- Check every download against the checksum the project publishes. When a project publishes none, record the SHA-256 you computed and say so in a comment.
- Install upstream release binaries. Do not build a tool from source to pick up a newer Go, Rust or library version.

## Vulnerabilities in bundled tools

- Findings inside an upstream binary are reported, not chased. A new upstream release reaches the image through the scheduled update.
- When a tool stops shipping releases and carries a critical finding that only a rebuild would fix, the maintainer decides whether to keep, drop or replace it. Record the decision in the pull request that makes it.

## Image and runtime

- Image-owned files live outside `/home/agent`. Initial, agent-owned `.profile` and `.bashrc` seed copies are the exception, so a newly created named home volume receives shell defaults. They become user files and startup does not replace them.
- The entrypoint never replaces a user's file with the image's copy; it only adds files that are missing. These exceptions each change only what they manage ([docs/running.md](docs/running.md#upgrading)):
  - `~/.agentainer/AGENTS.md` is replaced with a new image default only when it is a regular file the user never edited and `release_version.py newer-default` finds the image's release version newer than every version that shipped the current content (`30-agents-md.sh`). Local `dev` builds never replace it.
  - `agentainer-mcp sync` edits only the MCP servers recorded in `~/.agentainer/mcp-managed.json`.
  - `gh auth setup-git` and the git identity step write `~/.gitconfig`.
  - The OpenCode step runs `opencode service set disabled true` only when `~/.config/opencode/service.json` does not exist yet, which creates that file.
- Containers may share one home volume. Anything that writes to it must cope with another container doing the same at the same time (unique temp files, `flock`).
- Shell scripts are POSIX sh unless they need bash, and must pass `shellcheck` and `shfmt`. `/bin/sh` in the image is dash.

## Tests

- Add or change a test with each behavior change. A bug fix starts with a test that fails; run it and watch it fail before you fix the code.
- A test must be able to fail. A check that something is absent uses `assert_absent` with a marker that proves the command ran. Running the suite with `IMAGE=localhost/agentainer:no-such-image` must print no `ok` line.
- Container tests must not need the network unless the behavior is about the network. Use the fixtures in `tests/fixtures/`.
- Run the tests before asking for a commit, and report the real results, including failures.

## Git

- Follow the branch rules in [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). Never push to `main` and never run `git flow release finish`.
- Before each commit, show a file-by-file summary of what changed and wait for the maintainer's approval.
- When an AI agent writes a commit, end the message with a `Co-Authored-By` trailer that names that agent, with the address its maker documents for this purpose. Claude Code uses:

  ```
  Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
  ```

  If your maker documents no address, ask the maintainer before you commit.

- Sign maintainer-authored local commits and release tags with the configured signing key. Never disable signing to bypass a failure. Repo-local signing settings are not shared with contributors or CI.
- A release requires a signed annotated tag on the matching release merge in `main`. CI verifies it against `RELEASE_SIGNING_FINGERPRINT`; never put a private key in CI or the image.
- Do not force-push, rewrite published history, or delete branches without explicit instruction.

## Working on the host

- Do not install software on the maintainer's machine without asking first.
- Building and running containers locally is allowed. Remove the test containers, volumes and images you create.
- Do not deploy to any Kubernetes cluster without explicit approval for that deployment.

## Writing

These rules apply to docs, commit messages, pull request text, code comments and user-facing messages.

- Plain, direct sentences in active voice. Sentence-case headings.
- No em dashes. Use periods or commas.
- No filler ("in order to", "it is important to note"), no hype words ("seamless", "robust", "powerful"), no emojis.
- Say what a thing does, with the command, path or number, not how it feels.
- Code comments describe what the code does and why, as a developer would write them. No history ("now", "no longer", "fixed"), no references to reviews, tasks, plans or private notes.

# Setting up the agents

This page shows where each agent keeps its settings, instructions and skills inside the container, and how to set up status lines, plugins and MCP logins. Your settings, instructions and skills live under `/home/agent`, the persistent home, so they survive a new container. Run the commands inside the container (`bin/agentainer shell` or a tmux window).

The pinned versions are in [`versions.env`](../versions.env). The commands below were checked with `--help` in the image against Claude Code 2.1.309, Codex 0.166.0, Antigravity CLI 1.4.12 and OpenCode 2.2.5. [Signing in](logins.md) covers logins.

## Where each agent keeps things

| Agent | Settings | Global instructions | Personal skills |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `~/.claude/settings.json`; `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` moves it ([settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings)) | `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which imports the shared file | `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` |
| Codex | `~/.codex/config.toml`; `CODEX_HOME` moves it ([config reference](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-reference)) | `~/.codex/AGENTS.md`, a symlink to the shared file | `~/.agents/skills/` |
| Antigravity CLI | `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/settings.json` ([CLI reference](https://antigravity.google/docs/cli/reference#configuration-keys-settingsjson)) | `~/.gemini/AGENTS.md`, a symlink to the shared file | `~/.gemini/config/skills/` |
| OpenCode | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` and `cli.json`; `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` moves them ([config](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/config), [CLI settings](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli/config)) | `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`, a symlink to the shared file | `~/.config/opencode/skills/` |

- The shared instruction file is `~/.agentainer/AGENTS.md`. [AGENTS.md](configuration.md#agentsmd) explains the links, when the image updates the file, and what happens when one of these paths already holds your own file.
- [Default configuration](defaults.md#agent-configurations) lists what the image seeds in each settings file.
- `opencode debug paths` prints OpenCode's resolved config, data and cache directories.
- Agentainer's instruction links use the fixed instruction paths in this table and do not follow these variables.
- The MCP sync writes other files, such as `~/.claude.json` and `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json`. [MCP servers](configuration.md#mcp-servers) lists them; `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is the only override the sync follows.

## Skills

A skill is a directory with a `SKILL.md` file. Each agent reads personal skills from its own directories, and project skills from directories in the repository:

| Agent | Personal | Project | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `~/.claude/skills/` | `.claude/skills/` | [Claude skills](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills) |
| Codex | `~/.agents/skills/`; `/etc/codex/skills/` for admin skills | `.agents/skills/` from the working directory up to the repository root | [Codex skills](https://developers.openai.com/codex/skills) |
| Antigravity CLI | `~/.gemini/config/skills/`; the CLI also reads `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/skills/` and `~/.gemini/skills/` | `.agents/skills/` up to the repository root | [Antigravity skills](https://antigravity.google/docs/skills#cli-skill-locations) |
| OpenCode | `~/.config/opencode/skills/`; also `~/.claude/skills/` and `~/.agents/skills/` | `.opencode/skills/`, `.claude/skills/` and `.agents/skills/` | [OpenCode skills](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/skills#discovery) |

Not verified: discovery from these directories with the pinned CLIs. For OpenCode, an earlier check found that its skill API listed no copied skills ([plugins](plugins.md#opencode)).

Claude Code documents that a skill folder in its personal location can be a symlink to a directory elsewhere ([Claude skills](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills)). Whether the other agents follow symlinked skill directories is not verified.

The image's [unslop skill](configuration.md#writing-rules) is not registered as a native skill in any agent. The shared instructions tell agents to read it.

## Status lines

| Agent | What you can configure | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `statusLine` in `~/.claude/settings.json` runs a command. Claude passes session data as JSON on stdin and shows what the command prints. `/statusline` can write the script for you. | [Claude status line](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/statusline) |
| Codex | `tui.status_line` in `~/.codex/config.toml` is an ordered list of built-in footer items; `null` turns it off. `/statusline` opens a picker that writes the list. It does not run a custom command. | [Config reference](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-reference), [slash commands](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/cli/slash-commands.md) |
| Antigravity CLI | `statusLine` in `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/settings.json` runs a command with `sh -c`. The CLI passes session state as JSON on stdin and shows what the command prints. `stack_with_default` keeps the built-in line as well. | [Antigravity status line](https://antigravity.google/docs/cli/statusline) |
| OpenCode | `mini.footer` in `~/.config/opencode/cli.json` shows or hides the `opencode mini` footer (activity, model, usage and context). The image seeds `"footer": "show"`. `session.sidebar` is `auto` (show the sidebar when space permits) or `hide`. | [CLI settings](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli/config#mini), [sessions](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli/config#sessions) |

OpenCode's CLI settings page documents no custom status-line command; whether OpenCode 2.2.5 supports one is not verified.

For Claude Code and Antigravity, keep the script in the home volume so it survives a new container. For example, in `~/.claude/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "statusLine": {"type": "command", "command": "~/.claude/statusline.sh"}
}
```

Make the script executable with `chmod +x`. `jq` is in the image for reading the JSON input. No status line is seeded, and abtop does not install one ([monitoring](monitoring.md#model-calls-and-controls)). Not verified: custom status-line scripts with the pinned Claude Code and Antigravity versions.

## Plugins

[Optional plugins](plugins.md) has each agent's plugin commands and the checks to run after installing. Plugin settings and files under `/home/agent` survive a new container. Software a plugin needs outside the home must be installed again after the container is recreated.

## MCP servers and authentication

Define shared servers once in `~/.agentainer/mcp.json` and let `agentainer-mcp sync` write them into each agent ([MCP servers](configuration.md#mcp-servers)). Keep secrets in your env file and refer to them as `${NAME}`. How each agent receives a secret, and how it signs in to an OAuth server:

| Agent | `${NAME}` secrets from `mcp.json` | OAuth login for a remote server |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | Passed through | `claude mcp login <name>`; `--no-browser` prints the URL for a headless session ([Claude MCP](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp)) |
| Codex | `Authorization: Bearer ${NAME}` becomes `bearer_token_env_var`; other headers must be `${NAME}` alone | `codex mcp login <name>`; `--no-browser` prints the URL ([Codex MCP](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/extend/mcp)) |
| Antigravity CLI | Not written. The next sync rewrites a server it manages, so a header you add to it by hand does not survive. Add the server under a name that `mcp.json` does not use, with `agy mcp add --type http --header "Authorization: Bearer <token>" <name> <url>`. | Not verified. `agy mcp` has no login subcommand in 1.4.12 ([Antigravity MCP](https://antigravity.google/docs/mcp)). |
| OpenCode | Written as `{env:NAME}` | `opencode mcp auth [<name>]` ([OpenCode MCP](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/mcp-servers#oauth)) |

The sync accepts only the keys listed in [MCP servers](configuration.md#mcp-servers) and leaves out others, such as OAuth client settings, with a warning. Configure those in the agent itself, under a server name that `mcp.json` does not use. Not verified: completing an OAuth login in the container with any agent.

## Keeping settings across upgrades

Your settings, skills, plugins and logins stay in the home volume when you update the image. Startup changes only a few files; [upgrading](running.md#upgrading) lists them. To compare your files with new image defaults, look in `/etc/agentainer/home/`. To try changes without touching your main home, use a [separate test home](customization.md#image-upgrades-and-separate-test-homes).

# Agentainer environment

You are running inside an Agentainer container.

- Your project usually lives in `/workspace`. Only the paths mounted by the launcher or deployment are shared with the host or stored on volumes.
- Your home is `/home/agent`. Its contents survive container recreation when it is mounted from a persistent volume or host directory.
- `sudo` is usually disabled. If it works, packages installed with `apt` are lost when the container is recreated (for example on an image upgrade).
- Install extra tools in user space: `uv tool install`, `pipx install`, `npm install -g`, `cargo install` or `go install`. They go to `/var/lib/agentainer/active`. Whether they survive the container being recreated depends on `AGENTAINER_TOOLS` (`ephemeral` or `persist`).
- Python refuses `pip install --user` here (PEP 668). Use `uv`, `pipx` or a virtual environment.
- Credentials may come from environment variables or from agent login files in your home. Never print them, copy them into other files, or commit them.
- Follow the repository's commit, push and approval rules. Do not treat these environment instructions as permission to commit or push.

Edit this file to add your own instructions. It is `~/.agentainer/AGENTS.md`. Agentainer links each agent to it when that agent's own user instruction file is missing. If that file already exists, Agentainer leaves it as is, and the agent reads this file only if yours imports or links it.

## Files, documents and browsers

- In the Kubernetes example, `~/transfer` (`/home/agent/transfer`) is the folder a user reaches through the FileBrowser web file manager, and through SFTP when the operator turns it on. A user can upload a file there and give you its path. Outside that example `~/transfer` does not exist, and files arrive through `/workspace`.
- `pdftotext` extracts the text of a PDF, and `pdftoppm -png` renders its pages as images. ImageMagick (`magick`) converts and resizes images. It cannot read PDF or PostScript files, because the image has no ghostscript, so use `pdftoppm` for PDF pages.
- Chromium's OS libraries are in the image, so a browser needs no sudo. In a Playwright project, run `./node_modules/.bin/playwright install --only-shell chromium` as your user. For the Playwright MCP server, run `npx @playwright/mcp install-browser chromium`, and run it again after the server updates. Browsers download into your home. `/dev/shm` is the container engine's default size unless the deployment sets it (1 GiB in the Kubernetes example).

## Working rules

- Read the repository's instructions and inspect the relevant code before changing files. Follow its conventions and approval requirements.
- Never assume. Never guess. Always verify. Check commands, flags, paths and tool capabilities using installed help, official documentation or commands you run. State what you could not verify.
- If instructions are complicated or ambiguous and the intended outcome is unclear, ask the user what they want before proceeding with the affected work.
- Keep changes focused on the requested task. Preserve unrelated work and user-owned files.
- Run the checks relevant to the change. Report their actual results, including failures and checks you could not run. Do not claim a check passed unless you ran it or inspected its result.
- Never expose credentials or personal information in source code, logs, examples, commits or pull requests. Use generic placeholders in material intended for sharing.
- Describe what changed, why it changed and how you verified it. Identify any remaining limitations.

## Writing outside chat

For text covered below, read `/usr/local/share/agentainer/skills/unslop/SKILL.md` and apply its editing rules within this scope:

- Apply the full rules to docs, READMEs, plans, commit messages, PR and issue text, UI and marketing copy, user-facing errors, code comments and docstrings, and reports or other files written for the user. Short comment fragments and `TODO:` or `NOTE:` labels are allowed.
- Apply the full rules to instruction files, skills and memory notes, except the bold-formatting rule. Preserve required structures, including frontmatter and memory fields.
- For logs and internal errors, remove only obvious AI tells such as filler, fancy vocabulary, em dashes, emojis and chatbot phrases. Short, clipped wording is allowed.
- Exempt chat replies, including Insight blocks, machine-generated output such as lockfiles, generated code and build output, config keys and values, test fixture data, quotations and code identifiers.
- Apply the rules only to text you write or change. Do not reword untouched lines. Files written for the user remain covered even when created during a chat.

# Agentainer

Agentainer is one container image with four AI coding agents and a shared set of developer tools. You run it in a terminal on a laptop, a server or a Kubernetes cluster.

- Agents: [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup), [Codex CLI](https://github.com/openai/codex), [Antigravity CLI](https://antigravity.google/docs/overview?tab=cli) (`agy`) and [OpenCode v2](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs).
- Base: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, pinned by digest, with apt packages from the [Ubuntu snapshot service](https://documentation.ubuntu.com/server/how-to/software/snapshot-service/) at a pinned date.

## Quick start

You need Podman or Docker. The launcher [`bin/agentainer`](bin/agentainer) is a POSIX shell script.

Set `AGENTAINER_IMAGE` to a published version tag; no `latest` tag exists before the first stable release ([release versions](docs/versions.md#releases)). Or build locally with `scripts/build.sh` (`RUNTIME=docker sh scripts/build.sh` on a Docker host) and use `localhost/agentainer:dev`.

```sh
mkdir -p ~/.config/agentainer
cp env.example ~/.config/agentainer/env
chmod 600 ~/.config/agentainer/env      # then fill in the keys you use
export AGENTAINER_IMAGE=ghcr.io/chadmayfield/agentainer:0.1.0-dev.20261024.1
bin/agentainer up ~/code                 # ~/code becomes /workspace
bin/agentainer attach                    # tmux session "main"
```

Start an agent in a tmux window (`claude`, `codex`, `agy` or `opencode`). Close the terminal whenever you like. `bin/agentainer attach` brings you back to the same session with the agents still running.

# Visual color review

Generate terminal screenshots and an offline HTML gallery for human review. This is an optional test command. It does not build or publish an Agentainer image, modify a personal home, or call an agent API.

## Install the test dependencies

Use an existing Node.js installation compatible with the `engines` requirement in the locked Playwright package, Python 3, and Docker or Podman. The image must already be available locally. Capture uses `--pull=never` and `--network none`.

From the repository root:

```sh
cd tests/visual
npm ci --ignore-scripts
```

The exact test dependency versions and published integrity hashes are in `package.json` and `package-lock.json`. They were verified with `npm view PACKAGE version dist.integrity --json` against the npm registry. Nothing is added to the Agentainer runtime image. npm setup needs network access; terminal capture and rendering do not.

Dependabot checks these npm dependencies weekly and groups updates into one pull request against `develop`, with a seven-day cooldown. Review the lockfile changes and run the visual tests before merging ([Dependabot configuration](../../.github/dependabot.yml), [configuration reference](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/reference/supply-chain-security/dependabot-options-reference)).

## Generate the review

From `tests/visual/`, using an existing Chrome installation:

```sh
python3 capture.py --image localhost/agentainer:dev
BROWSER_CHANNEL=chrome npm run screenshots
```

To review changes to home defaults before rebuilding, use an existing compatible image and overlay this checkout's defaults read-only:

```sh
python3 capture.py --image localhost/agentainer:dev --source-defaults
BROWSER_CHANNEL=chrome npm run screenshots
```

`--source-defaults` changes only the mounted home seed files and shared instructions. It does not test changes to the Containerfile or entrypoint. The gallery labels the defaults as either `image` or `checkout overlay`. An overlay preview does not verify a newly built image.

Use `--runtime docker` for Docker Engine, or set `RUNTIME=docker`. `IMAGE` can supply the image reference instead of `--image`. These invocation options are documented by `python3 capture.py --help`; container flags were verified with `podman run --help` and the [Docker run reference](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/).

`BROWSER_CHANNEL=chrome` selects installed Google Chrome. With an existing Playwright Chromium installation, omit that variable. The command does not install browsers automatically. Follow [Playwright's browser documentation](https://playwright.dev/docs/browsers) to install a browser if needed. Do not install one on someone else's machine without their approval.

Open `artifacts/visual/index.html` relative to the repository root. It embeds every screenshot and opens directly from disk without JavaScript, a web server, external fonts or a CDN. The page uses the GitHub Dark shared roles, `#010409` background and `#e6edf3` text, in either client color scheme. The terminal screenshots keep their captured colors. A Markdown companion, `artifacts/visual/index.md`, links to individual PNGs in `artifacts/visual/screenshots/`. Commit the Markdown and its PNGs together, preserving their relative paths, for GitHub rendering ([GitHub relative image paths](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/getting-started-with-writing-and-formatting-on-github/basic-writing-and-formatting-syntax#relative-links)). Generating them does not commit or publish them. The HTML, raw terminal recordings in `captures.json`, temporary output and `tests/visual/node_modules/` remain gitignored. Generated HTML and screenshots include font-rendered pixels, not redistributed font files.

Check both command exit codes. A failed capture or render does not replace the previous complete capture or gallery. An old gallery can remain after a failed run.

## Coverage

| Tool | States |
|---|---|
| Shell and ls | Prompt, normal files, directory, symbolic link, executable; every file type ls colors, including setuid, setgid, sticky and other-writable directories, a broken link, a pipe, a socket and `/dev/null` |
| eza | Long listing with metadata and Git indicators; nested tree; working and broken symbolic links |
| Git | Mixed staged, modified, deleted and untracked status; working-tree diff; staged diff; real unresolved merge conflict |
| bat | Python and YAML syntax with its configured ANSI theme |
| fzf | Empty query; matching query; multiple selections; no matches |
| Vim | Python; YAML; search matches and trailing whitespace; visual selection; right-hand browser at 120 and 80 columns |
| tmux | Single pane; multiple windows and split panes; copy-mode selection; background-window activity; split panes at 80 columns |

There are 26 captured terminal states. The `ls-colors` state creates each file type the agent user can create in a temporary directory and lists it with `ls -ld --color=always`, beside `/dev/null`. The agent user cannot create a block device, because `mknod` needs a capability, so the last row applies the `bd` style from `$LS_COLORS` to a sample name and labels it "illustrated". Dates are hidden in that state, because the `/dev/null` date comes from the container runtime. Each captured case records actual tool output through a Linux pseudo-terminal, including full-screen applications before they exit. The browser replays that output in [xterm.js](https://xtermjs.org/docs/api/terminal/classes/terminal/) and uses [Playwright element screenshots](https://playwright.dev/docs/screenshots#element-screenshot). The test checks expected text on the rendered screen, colored text, loaded fonts, browser errors, and that all embedded images load. It checks explicit background colors, such as selections and special permissions, the tmux activity text color, and that the zero-result fzf screen contains no candidate names. Missing scenarios or incomplete recordings fail the run. The Markdown checks verify relative image paths and escape captured text. It does not compare screenshots against approved baselines.

The fixture uses generic files and identity inside the disposable container. It creates temporary Git history there, never in the host repository. All containers are named `cx-visual-*`; capture runs one container at a time and removes it when finished or on timeout. No personal home, credentials, container socket or real project is mounted. The optional source overlay mounts only the two documented seed paths.

The renderer fixes most terminals at 120 columns by 32 rows, with the two narrow views at 80 columns by 24 rows. Each screenshot is labeled with its dimensions. It uses the locked JetBrains Mono font at 14px, and supplies the GitHub Dark reference ANSI palette, copied from `TERMINAL` in [`tests/unit/palette.py`](../unit/palette.py), with cursor `#f78166`. Truecolor escapes come from the captured programs. bat's ANSI colors depend on this reference palette and may differ in a user's terminal. Sample file dates, Git dates and the tmux time and date are fixed. The tmux capture reads the configured `status-right` and replaces `%H:%M` with `12:00` and `%x` with `10/19/26`, so every block renders as configured. Browser and operating-system rendering can still differ ([Playwright rendering limits](https://playwright.dev/docs/test-snapshots)). The renderer records its browser version in the gallery. Local execution used Podman on arm64 with installed Chrome and a locally built image. Docker Engine and amd64 execution are not verified.

Agent client interfaces, real authentication, shell completion menus and live clipboard transfer are not verified by this gallery. A human should inspect text contrast, selection visibility, gutters and status lines in the gallery, then confirm the result in their own terminal. Generation is not visual approval.

## Release use

Keep this command optional until it has been reviewed. For a release, run it against the already built candidate image without `--source-defaults` and review the resulting gallery. A separate Agentainer build is unnecessary. No release or pull-request workflow is enabled by this change.

The same command can later run manually in CI or on configuration pull requests and upload `artifacts/visual/`, including both gallery formats and the PNGs. Browser dependencies belong in the test environment. Release-only execution would miss useful feedback while colors are being changed.

## Branches

The repo uses git-flow:

- `develop` is the default branch. Open pull requests against it.
- Work on a `feature/<name>` branch made from `develop` (`git flow feature start <name>`, or `git switch -c feature/<name> develop`).
- `main` holds releases and changes only through release pull requests.
- Merged branches are deleted automatically. Merge with "Create a merge commit"; squash and rebase merges are turned off. These are repository settings in GitHub, not files in this repository.

## Build and test

You need Podman or Docker.

```sh

sh tests/run.sh                             # container tests against that image
sh tests/lint.sh                            # shellcheck, shfmt and Ruff, run from the image
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests/unit  # unit tests, no container needed

sh tests/host/test-fetch.sh                 # fetch.sh and Rust manifest check tests, no container needed

sh tests/host/test-launcher-integration.sh  # real engine, existing local image
sh tests/host/test-build-uid.sh             # slow: builds a full image with --uid 1001 --gid 20
python3 tests/host/test-layer-repro.py      # slow: two clean tool builds, configured Buildx
python3 tests/host/test-healthcheck.py      # also invoked by tests/58-healthcheck.sh
python3 tests/host/test-language-tooling.py --image localhost/agentainer:dev  # slow, network
```

With Docker, prefix the commands with `RUNTIME=docker`. `IMAGE=<name>` tests another image. Two tests do not follow both settings:

- `tests/host/test-layer-repro.py` always runs `docker buildx`.
- `tests/host/test-build-uid.sh` builds and tests its own image tag. On a build failure it prints the last 80 lines of the build output.

### Python linting

`sh tests/lint.sh` runs Ruff from the built image alongside shellcheck and shfmt. CI runs the same command in each architecture's image job. Rebuild the image after changing its Ruff pin. No host Ruff installation is required.

[`ruff.toml`](ruff.toml) selects only Pyflakes `F` rules. [`scripts/lint-python.py`](scripts/lint-python.py) includes `.py` files and Python shebang commands in the source directories, including `build/` and extensionless runtime commands. It excludes dependency and cache directories. Explicit file arguments prevent Ruff's default exclusion of `build/` from hiding those scripts ([Ruff file discovery](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/configuration/#python-file-discovery), [Pyflakes rules](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/#pyflakes-f)).

### Kelos variant

[`Containerfile.kelos`](Containerfile.kelos) builds a variant image for Kelos on top of a published Agentainer image ([docs/kelos.md](docs/kelos.md)). Its files are in `rootfs-kelos/` and its tests in `tests/kelos/`.

```sh
scripts/build.sh --variant kelos [--from IMAGE]                       # builds localhost/agentainer-kelos:dev
IMAGE=localhost/agentainer-kelos:dev sh tests/kelos/test_image.sh     # tests for the variant
```

Without `--from`, the build uses the digest-pinned image named in `Containerfile.kelos`. The `kelos-capture` stage needs network access to github.com and the Go module proxy. CI does not build or test the variant.

## CI

[`.github/workflows/build.yml`](.github/workflows/build.yml) runs on every pull request, every push to `develop` and `main`, and every `v*` tag push. A pull request also runs it again when you edit it, which includes changing its base branch:

- the `lint-unit` job: actionlint, the Python unit tests, and the launcher, `scripts/build.sh` and `build/fetch.sh` tests;
- the `image` job, on amd64 and arm64: the image build, shellcheck and shfmt (`tests/lint.sh` runs them from the image), the container tests and real launcher lifecycle under Docker and rootless Podman, a custom UID/GID build, the manifest tests, and trivy scans (a secret fails the build; vulnerabilities are reported). On amd64 only, it also checks that the four agents and Node.js start on a CPU without AVX2.

The `layer-repro` job runs on amd64 and arm64 and uses the pinned BuildKit image to build an isolated copy of every tool twice with no cache. It compares the exported tool-layer digests. This checks unchanged inputs; it does not test every possible combination of pin changes. The required `ci` check includes this job.

The image and layer comparison jobs are skipped when every changed file is `README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `SECURITY.md`, `LICENSE` or a file under `docs/` other than `docs/kubernetes.md` (the manifest tests check its install commands). For a pull request, the changed files are what the merge adds to the base branch. For a push to `develop`, they are the files changed since the previous tip. A push to `main` and a pull request whose base branch changed always build the image. A docs-only change gets no shell lint, because no shell file changed. The required check is `ci`, which passes only when every job passed or the image job was skipped for a docs-only change.

The manual [optional tooling workflow](.github/workflows/optional-tooling.yml) (`workflow_dispatch`) builds the selected source and runs the networked language-server and Playwright installation checks with Docker on amd64 and arm64 runners. It has read-only repository permission and is separate from the required `ci` check. Not verified: it has no runs yet (`gh run list --workflow optional-tooling.yml` returns none).

## Signing local commits

Configure signing once in your checkout, with your own full GPG fingerprint and a key whose UID uses your GitHub noreply address:

```sh
git config --local user.signingkey YOUR_FULL_GPG_FINGERPRINT
git config --local gpg.format openpgp
git config --local commit.gpgsign true
git config --local tag.gpgsign true
```

These settings stay in `.git/config`, apply to this local clone and its worktrees, and are not shared with contributors or other clones. Register the public key on your GitHub account so GitHub can verify signatures. Keep the private key on your signing host. A signing failure stops the commit; fix access to the key instead of disabling signing. Verify a new commit with `git verify-commit HEAD` ([Git configuration](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config), [commit verification](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-verify-commit)). GitHub-generated merge commits and automated bump commits use their own identities.

## Releases

1. From an up-to-date `develop` whose CI passed, run `git flow release start <version>`. Use SemVer, such as `0.1.0`, or a dated development prerelease, such as `0.1.0-dev.20261019.1` ([version policy](docs/versions.md#releases)).
2. Push the branch and open a pull request from `release/<version>` to `main`.
3. When `ci` passes, merge with "Create a merge commit". The subject must be exactly `Merge pull request #N from <owner>/release/<version>`. A push to `main` tests the merge but does not publish.
4. Fetch the merged commit, create a signed annotated tag `v<version>` on that exact merge commit with `git tag -s v<version> <merge-commit> -m "Release v<version>"`, verify it with `git verify-tag v<version>`, then push only that tag with `git push origin refs/tags/v<version>` ([signed tags](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-tag)). Do not tag the release branch's pre-merge tip.
5. The tag push runs CI. After aggregate CI passes, `scripts/check_release_tag.py` requires a two-parent release merge on main's first-parent history, a matching tag version and target, and a valid GPG signature by the trusted primary key. It retrieves the owner's public key from GitHub and verifies in a temporary keyring. Set the repository Actions variable `RELEASE_SIGNING_FINGERPRINT` to that full uppercase fingerprint. The signing key must be registered on the repository owner's GitHub account, or on the account named by the optional `RELEASE_SIGNER` Actions variable for an organization-owned repository ([public GPG keys API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/users/gpg-keys)). A missing key setting, unsigned tag or existing GitHub release stops publishing. The version job checks out `main` to run this check, so a candidate tag cannot replace it.
6. Approve the `authorize-release` job in the `release` environment. Then the workflow:
   1. Builds and pushes both architectures.
   2. On each native runner, pulls the pushed digest, checks the image architecture, source revision and release version, and starts the image and all four agent binaries before uploading its digest artifact ([platform check](scripts/check-release-platform.sh)). A failure stops index publication and promotion.
   3. Assembles an index tagged only `sha-<short>`, signs it and the platform manifests with cosign, and creates a GitHub provenance attestation for the index, stored in GitHub and GHCR.
   4. Runs [`tests/host/test-published-image.py`](tests/host/test-published-image.py): exact workflow identity, source commit and tag ref for GitHub provenance; expected repository and commit in each platform's BuildKit provenance; signatures, SBOM descriptors and native startup.
   5. Only after that verification, moves the version tag, and `latest` for the highest stable version (see [moving `latest`](#moving-latest)).
   6. Creates the GitHub release with `--verify-tag`, keeping the maintainer-signed tag. Prereleases are marked as prereleases and excluded from latest.
7. Open a pull request from `main` to `develop` to bring back fixes made on the release branch.

Do not run `git flow release finish`: it merges into `main` locally. A hotfix is a new release made the same way. A `hotfix/*` merge does not authorize publication.

Re-run a failed tag workflow without replacing the signed tag. A failure before verification and the retag dry run pass leaves the version and `latest` tags unchanged. A rebuilt image gets a new digest; it must be signed, attested and verified again before promotion. Once the GitHub release exists, its version cannot be republished. Use a new version for further changes.

CI holds no maintainer private signing key. It verifies the GPG-signed release tag using the maintainer's public key, then uses GitHub OIDC for container image signatures and attestations.

The published image is a fresh build from the release commit with the same pinned inputs, not the exact image the pull request's tests ran on. The verifier checks the named fields; it does not establish a SLSA level or validate every SBOM package entry. Fixtures exercise rejection cases in pull requests.

### Moving latest

The release job refreshes `main` while holding its release lock. Only the highest stable SemVer in main's first-parent release merges can move `latest`. Prereleases never move it, even when they target a higher version. A delayed older stable build or retry publishes its own version tag and leaves `latest` alone. Ordering is numeric, so `0.1.10` follows `0.1.2`, and `0.1.0-dev.20261019.10` follows `0.1.0-dev.20261019.2`. A version without a prerelease suffix follows every prerelease of that same version ([release script](scripts/release-image.sh), [version comparison](scripts/release_order.py)). GitHub releases use the same decision ([GitHub CLI release flags](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_release_create)).

### Release concurrency

The release job's concurrency group keeps one running job and one pending job. Under GitHub's default policy, a third queued release replaces the pending one. Check all pushed tags and rerun any canceled release workflow ([concurrency](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/workflows-and-actions/concurrency)). GitHub documents larger queues; whether the pinned actionlint accepts that setting is not verified.

### GitHub release controls

These controls are GitHub repository settings. The workflow files cannot enforce them, so an administrator must configure them:

- The `release` environment requires the maintainer's approval and permits only `v*` tags. Self-approval is allowed so a sole maintainer can release. The `authorize-release` job waits for that approval before the publish jobs run ([environment protection](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/deployments-and-environments)).
- A tag ruleset blocks updates and deletion of `v*` tags, without bypass actors, and permits new tags. Correct a released version by creating a new version instead of replacing its tag ([ruleset rules](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/available-rules-for-rulesets)).
- Protect `main` and release-tag creation.
- Fork pull-request workflows require approval for all external contributors. Review their changes before approving a run ([fork workflow approval](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/approve-runs-from-forks)).

## The bump GitHub App

The scheduled update ([`.github/workflows/bump.yml`](.github/workflows/bump.yml)) opens its pull request with a GitHub App token, so CI starts without "Approve workflows to run". To set the App up:

1. Under your account's Settings, Developer settings, GitHub Apps, create a new App. Use the repository URL as its homepage and turn off its webhook.
2. Give it the repository permissions Contents (read and write) and Pull requests (read and write), and nothing else. Allow installing it only on your account.
3. Copy its Client ID (not the App ID) and generate a private key.
4. Install the App on the `agentainer` repository only.
5. In the repository's Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions, add the variable `BUMP_APP_CLIENT_ID` (the Client ID) and the secret `BUMP_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` (the whole `.pem` file). Then delete the downloaded key file.
6. Run `gh workflow run bump.yml`. If it opens a pull request, its CI starts on its own, and the commit author is the App's bot user.

The workflow uses the App only when both the variable and the secret are set. If either is missing, it uses `GITHUB_TOKEN`. With both set, wrong App credentials fail the App job without falling back; remove the variable or the secret to go back to `GITHUB_TOKEN`.

## Reporting a vulnerability

Report vulnerabilities privately through GitHub: open the repository's **Security** tab and choose **Report a vulnerability**. Do not open a public issue for a security problem.

Include what you found, how to reproduce it, and the exact image reference you used, with its tag or digest (for example `ghcr.io/chadmayfield/agentainer@sha256:...`). This command shows the image's version label, which helps but does not identify the image on its own; a local build reports `dev`:

```sh
docker image inspect <image> --format '{{index .Config.Labels "org.opencontainers.image.version"}}'
```

## What is in scope

- The image build: `Containerfile`, `build/`, and the pins in `versions.env`.
- The scripts the image ships in `rootfs/`, such as the entrypoint and `agentainer-mcp`.
- The launcher `bin/agentainer`.
- The Kubernetes example in `deploy/kubernetes/`, including the auth webhook.
- The Kelos variant: `Containerfile.kelos`, `rootfs-kelos/` and `tests/kelos/`.

A vulnerability in an agent or tool that the image installs (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI, OpenCode, Go, gh and the others) belongs to that project. Report it there. Once the project ships a fix, a scheduled or manually triggered version bump brings it into the image.

## Supported versions

Fixes ship in new releases; older images are not rebuilt under the same version. Releases use SemVer, including dated development prereleases such as `0.1.0-dev.20261019.1`. The image tag `latest` follows the highest stable release. Prereleases require an explicit version tag, and `latest` does not exist before the first stable release. See the [release policy](docs/versions.md#releases).

## Known limits

[docs/security.md](docs/security.md) lists what the container does and does not isolate. Every supplied credential is available to container code, and agents can modify mounted files that the host later executes. The example ContainerSSH webhook serves plain HTTP. TLS requires server-side changes or a TLS-terminating proxy; there is no webhook TLS switch.

Each release lists its trivy findings in the release notes and attaches the full reports ([docs/security.md](docs/security.md#vulnerability-reports)).

# Optional browser testing Install Playwright in the project that needs it. Agentainer supplies Node.js, npm and the OS libraries and fonts that Playwright lists for Chromium on Ubuntu 26.04 (`nativeDeps.ts` in Playwright v1.64.1, without `xvfb`). The browsers themselves are not in the image. They download into your home as the `agent` user, with no sudo. Playwright supports Ubuntu 26.04 on amd64 and arm64 ([system requirements](https://playwright.dev/docs/intro#system-requirements)). Follow an existing project's package-manager instructions and lockfile instead of creating a second setup. ## Contents - [Install the project dependency and browser](#install-the-project-dependency-and-browser) - [Verify execution](#verify-execution) - [Other browsers and older images](#other-browsers-and-older-images) - [The Playwright MCP plugin](#the-playwright-mcp-plugin) - [Shared memory and network access](#shared-memory-and-network-access) - [Updates, recreation and cleanup](#updates-recreation-and-cleanup) - [Verify the Agentainer instructions](#verify-the-agentainer-instructions) ## Install the project dependency and browser Inside the container, enter the project directory under `/workspace`. For a new, empty npm project: ```sh npm init --yes npm install --save-dev --save-exact @playwright/test export PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH="$HOME/.cache/ms-playwright" ./node_modules/.bin/playwright install --only-shell chromium ``` Keep `package.json` and `package-lock.json` in version control. For an existing locked npm project, use `npm ci` instead of the first two commands. Run the browser download as the normal `agent` user. See [Playwright installation](https://playwright.dev/docs/intro) and [npm dependency locking](project-tools.md#javascript-dependencies-and-package-manager-versions). Browser binaries must match the project's Playwright version ([Playwright browser requirements](https://playwright.dev/docs/browsers)). `--only-shell chromium` downloads Chromium's headless shell. It supports headless tests without a browser channel selection. Headed tests, code generation with a visible browser, or a configuration using `channel: 'chromium'` need the full browser instead: run `./node_modules/.bin/playwright install chromium`. The image has no X server (`xvfb` is left out), so a headed browser needs a display from somewhere else ([browser installation choices](https://playwright.dev/docs/browsers#chromium-headless-shell)). Use the same `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` when installing and running tests. Export it in each shell that runs Playwright, or add the export to your own container `~/.bashrc`. `~/.cache/ms-playwright` is on the home volume in either tools mode; `AGENTAINER_TOOLS=persist` is not required. It stores executables, not browser login sessions ([browser storage](https://playwright.dev/docs/browsers#managing-browser-binaries)). ## Verify execution Create `browser-smoke.spec.cjs` in the project: ```js const { test, expect } = require('@playwright/test'); test('Chromium renders, handles input and captures a screenshot', async ({ page }, testInfo) => { await page.route('**/*', route => route.abort()); await page.setContent('

Browser ready

'); await expect(page.getByRole('heading')).toHaveText('Browser ready'); await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Try it' }).click(); await expect(page.getByRole('button')).toHaveText('Clicked'); await page.screenshot({ path: testInfo.outputPath('browser-smoke.png') }); }); ``` Run it with the project-local command: ```sh ./node_modules/.bin/playwright test browser-smoke.spec.cjs --workers=1 --reporter=line ``` The test renders a page, clicks a button, checks its new text and writes `browser-smoke.png` under `test-results/`. It aborts page network requests and needs no external website. A browser launch failure or failed assertion returns a nonzero exit code. See [test assertions](https://playwright.dev/docs/test-assertions), [request interception](https://playwright.dev/docs/network#handle-requests) and [screenshots](https://playwright.dev/docs/screenshots). On 2026-11-04 this test passed in the [Kubernetes example](kubernetes.md) pod under the Restricted Pod Security Standard, with the optional egress policy on, using `@playwright/test` 1.64.1 and `playwright install --only-shell chromium`. It wrote a valid PNG. For an existing project, follow its Playwright configuration and test command. A development server inside the container can listen on `0.0.0.0`; use the launcher's [port publishing](running.md#development-server-ports) to open it in a host browser. ## Other browsers and older images The image carries Chromium's libraries only. Firefox and WebKit need their own downloads and OS dependencies, and images older than this change have no browser libraries at all. Both cases need root for `install-deps`. The launcher blocks sudo by default, so create a container with `--sudo` for that step, or use a [custom image](customization.md#customize-the-image-itself) that already has the libraries ([Linux dependencies](https://playwright.dev/docs/browsers#install-system-dependencies)). Select an available image as described in [running Agentainer](running.md), then run this from the repository root for a separate browser-testing home: ```sh AGENTAINER_HOME_VOLUME=agentainer-browser-home \ bin/agentainer up --sudo --name agentainer-browser "$HOME/code" bin/agentainer shell agentainer-browser ``` `$HOME/code` must exist on the host. Inside the container, install the libraries before the browser, for example for Firefox: ```sh sudo ./node_modules/.bin/playwright install-deps firefox ./node_modules/.bin/playwright install firefox ``` The home volume keeps browser downloads. OS libraries installed with sudo live in the container's writable layer. Repeat their installation when replacing the container, or include them in your custom image. The launcher keeps `--sudo` during updates ([launcher options](running.md#the-launcher)). ## The Playwright MCP plugin Claude Code's Playwright plugin starts `npx @playwright/mcp@latest` with no arguments ([its `.mcp.json`](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-plugins-official/blob/main/external_plugins/playwright/.mcp.json)). The image's Claude Code has the built-in `anthropic-plugin-directory` marketplace (`claude plugin marketplace list`), so this works with no marketplace step: ```sh claude plugin install playwright@anthropic-plugin-directory --scope user ``` `playwright@claude-plugins-official` installs the same plugin after you add that marketplace as described in [plugins.md](plugins.md#claude-code). The server's default browser is the `chrome` channel, which the image does not have. The image sets `PLAYWRIGHT_MCP_BROWSER=chromium`, which `@playwright/mcp` reads as its `--browser` option, so the server uses Playwright's own Chromium build. With no `DISPLAY` set, the server runs the browser headless. Before the first use, download the browser that the server's Playwright version expects: ```sh npx @playwright/mcp install-browser chromium ``` - The plugin follows `@latest`, so the browser build it needs changes when a new server release comes out. Rerun the command after an update, and when a tool call reports a missing browser. - The command downloads a full Chromium build plus a headless shell and ffmpeg into `~/.cache/ms-playwright`, separate from your projects' browsers. With `@playwright/mcp` 0.0.84 on arm64 that was 692 MB (`chromium-1252` 407 MB, `chromium_headless_shell-1252` 281 MB, `ffmpeg-1013` 3.9 MB). Each new build adds another set to your home. `du -sh ~/.cache/ms-playwright/*` shows what is there. - Pinning the plugin to a fixed `@playwright/mcp` version is your choice. The image does not do it. Verified with `@playwright/mcp` 0.0.84: `tests/host/test-playwright-setup.py` lists the server's 25 tools, opens a page on `127.0.0.1` and takes a screenshot. The same check passed in the Kubernetes example pod on 2026-11-04 ("mcp-ok tools=25"). ## Shared memory and network access Chromium uses `/dev/shm`. Playwright's Docker guide recommends `--ipc=host` and says "Without it, Chromium can run out of memory and crash" ([Playwright Docker docs](https://playwright.dev/docs/docker)). The launcher keeps the engine's default size, which is 64 MB under Podman (`df -h /dev/shm` shows 63M). The smoke test and the MCP check pass with that size. For pages that need more, run the container without the launcher and add `--shm-size=1g` ([without the launcher](running.md#without-the-launcher), `man podman-run`). The Kubernetes example mounts a 1 GiB memory-backed volume at `/dev/shm`, which counts against the agent container's memory limit ([shared memory](kubernetes.md#shared-memory)). Under the Kubernetes example's optional egress policy, the pod reaches public addresses on TCP 443 only. Plain HTTP on port 80 is blocked, so test against `https://` URLs or a server inside the pod. The npm registry and the Playwright download CDN use 443, and `npx -y @playwright/mcp@0.0.84 install-browser chromium` worked under that policy on 2026-11-04 ([network policy](kubernetes.md#network-policy)). ## Updates, recreation and cleanup After updating the project's Playwright version, repeat the browser install command. Playwright versions select matching browser revisions. After replacing the container, restore the project's dependencies with `npm ci` if needed and export the same browser path. Browser files remain on the persistent home, and the new container's image supplies the libraries. Reinstall browser files and project dependencies when changing architecture. See [Playwright browser versions](https://playwright.dev/docs/browsers) and [project environment portability](customization.md#project-dependencies-and-installed-tools). Playwright removes unused browser revisions as clients are updated. `./node_modules/.bin/playwright install --list` shows installed browsers; `./node_modules/.bin/playwright uninstall` removes browsers for that Playwright installation. Avoid `uninstall --all` when other projects or the MCP plugin share the browser directory ([browser management](https://playwright.dev/docs/browsers#stale-browser-removal)). Keep `node_modules/`, `test-results/` and any generated `playwright-report/` out of the project's Git history. Browser authentication state, traces and screenshots can contain application data; store and publish only the outputs you intend to share ([authentication state](https://playwright.dev/docs/auth)). ## Verify the Agentainer instructions From this repository root, run the optional networked setup check against an existing local image: ```sh python3 tests/host/test-playwright-setup.py --image localhost/agentainer:dev ``` Use `--runtime docker` for Docker Engine. The check does the following: - Runs the containers with `--security-opt no-new-privileges`, so sudo cannot gain root. - Installs the Playwright version locked for [visual tests](../tests/visual/package.json) and Chromium's headless shell as the `agent` user. - Runs the smoke test, and checks that a deliberately wrong assertion fails. - Recreates the container with the same home and workspace volumes, checks the browser file hashes and runs the test again. - Installs the MCP server's browser with `npx @playwright/mcp@0.0.84 install-browser chromium`, checks that the project's browser files keep their hashes, then starts the server, lists its tools, opens a local page and takes a screenshot. - Creates one container at a time, uses only `cx-*` names and removes its containers and volumes. It does not build an image or mount a personal home. Setup needs network access to npm and the Playwright downloads. The smoke test itself blocks page network requests. The manual workflow [`.github/workflows/optional-tooling.yml`](../.github/workflows/optional-tooling.yml) (`workflow_dispatch`) builds the image and runs this check and the [language tooling check](language-tooling.md#updates-and-verification) with Docker on amd64 and arm64 runners. Not verified: the workflow has no runs yet (`gh run list --workflow optional-tooling.yml` returns none). See [CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md#ci).

## AGENTS.md

You keep one instruction file, `~/.agentainer/AGENTS.md`. Agentainer connects each agent to it:

| Agent | Reads | How |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` | Contains `@~/.agentainer/AGENTS.md` ([imports](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory)) |
| Codex | `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` | Symlink |
| Antigravity | `~/.gemini/AGENTS.md` | Symlink |
| OpenCode | `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md` | Symlink |

The entrypoint seeds `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` and creates each symlink only when that path is missing. An existing `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is kept without a message. An existing regular file at one of the three symlink paths is kept with a warning. In both cases that agent reads the shared file only if your file imports or links it.

The seeded Claude settings set `instructionFiles` to `claude-md-and-agents-md`, so Claude Code loads both `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` in a repo that has both ([instruction files setting](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory)). Each repo's own `AGENTS.md` still loads on top of yours.

The first start copies the image's default. A later image replaces your copy with its own default only when all of these hold:

- You never edited the file. It still matches a default this home has seen.
- The file is a regular file. A symlinked `~/.agentainer/AGENTS.md`, for example from a dotfiles repo, is never replaced.
- The image has a release version (`AGENTAINER_IMAGE_VERSION`), not a local build (`dev`).
- That version is newer than every recorded version that shipped your file's content. A prerelease can replace an older prerelease default, but never a default that a stable release shipped.

Release versions follow [SemVer](https://semver.org/), including dated development builds such as `0.1.0-dev.20261019.1`. A replacement keeps the file mode and prints one line. In every other case the file is not touched. If the image's default is one this home has not seen before, the entrypoint prints one notice; `agentainer-agents diff` shows the difference.

`~/.agentainer/agents-default.sha256` records every default the home has seen, one line per default and image version: `<sha256> <version>`. A line with only a hash comes from an image that did not record its version and counts as older than any release. So an older image never rolls the file back, and two images that share one home volume do not report each other's default more than once.

### Writing rules

The shared default tells agents to read `/usr/local/share/agentainer/skills/unslop/SKILL.md` before writing covered text. This is one image-owned copy of [Cursor's unslop skill](https://github.com/cursor/plugins/tree/main/pstack/skills/unslop), with the upstream [MIT license and attribution](https://github.com/cursor/plugins/blob/main/pstack/LICENSE). The build verifies both files against the commit and SHA-256 values in [`versions.env`](../versions.env). Upstream publishes no checksum files for these sources; the updater computes the recorded hashes from the same immutable commit.

The shared instructions set this scope:

| Content | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Docs, READMEs, plans, commits, PRs, issues, UI and marketing copy, user-facing errors, comments, docstrings and files written for the user | Full editing rules; short comment fragments and `TODO:` or `NOTE:` labels are allowed |
| Instruction files, skills and memory notes | Full rules except the bold-formatting rule; required structures stay intact |
| Logs and internal errors | Remove obvious AI tells; clipped wording is allowed |
| Chat replies and Insight blocks | Exempt |
| Generated output, lockfiles, generated code, config keys and values, test fixture data, quotations and code identifiers | Exempt |
| Untouched text | Leave unchanged |

Edit the writing section in `~/.agentainer/AGENTS.md` to customize or disable it. Homes with edited instructions or a local `dev` image keep their copy; compare the new section with `agentainer-agents diff` before adopting it.

Agentainer references the skill through the shared instructions. It does not register a native `/unslop` command or install the rest of pstack. Whether models follow the writing rules is not verified.

## MCP servers

Define servers once in `~/.agentainer/mcp.json`, in the `mcpServers` format most MCP server READMEs use:

```json
{"mcpServers": {
  "remote": {"url": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp", "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ${EXAMPLE_TOKEN}"}},
  "everything": {"command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything@2.0.0"]}
}}
```

The sample fixes the package version using [published npm metadata](https://registry.npmjs.org/@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything/2.0.0). Stdio MCP servers execute code with the filesystem access and environment their agent gives them. Review the server and its dependencies before adding it. Use explicit package versions or a locked local installation.

`agentainer-mcp sync` writes them into each agent's own configuration:

| Agent | Where |
|---|---|
| Claude Code | `mcpServers` in `~/.claude.json`, or `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/.claude.json` |
| Codex | `[mcp_servers.<name>]` tables in a marked block at the end of `~/.codex/config.toml` |
| Antigravity | `mcpServers` in `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json` |
| OpenCode | `mcp.servers` in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` |

The JSON paths and formats match output from `claude mcp add-json --scope user` and `agy mcp add`, checked in the image. Claude documents its [user scope](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp).

When the sync runs:

- On container start, when `mcp.json` changed. Startup runs `agentainer-mcp sync --if-changed`.
- When you run `agentainer-mcp sync`, even if `mcp.json` did not change.
- A failed write leaves no success stamp, so the next start retries.

Ownership:

- `~/.agentainer/mcp-managed.json` records which servers the sync added, for all four agents. The sync adds, updates and removes only those servers and never touches servers you added yourself. `agentainer-mcp list` shows them.
- Deleting `mcp.json` removes the servers the sync added.
- Config files that are symlinks stay symlinks; the sync writes the file the link points to.
- Direct and startup syncs share one lock, so they run one at a time on a shared home volume. The lock does not coordinate with agents that write the same files, so stop those agents before you sync.
- A journal records config hashes and managed names before each write, so a restart can recover ownership after an interrupted sync. If the config changed during that interruption, the sync stops for inspection instead of claiming ownership.

Server names may use only letters, digits, `-` and `_`. Any other name stops the sync with an error such as `agentainer-mcp: server name 'my.server' may only use letters, digits, - and _; nothing changed`.

A server entry has these keys:

| Kind | Keys | `type` |
|---|---|---|
| Command | `command`, `args`, `env` | `stdio` (optional) |
| URL | `url`, `headers` | `http` (default) or `sse` |

Any other `type` stops the sync with an error and changes nothing. Other keys, such as `cwd`, `timeout` or `disabled`, are not passed on; the sync prints a warning naming them.

Keep secrets as `${NAME}` references to variables in your env file; no agent config receives the value. The sync writes literal values directly into agent config files and never passes server configuration to a child process. New config files have mode `0600`. Existing files keep their permissions unless a sync writes literal environment or header values; those writes remove group and other permissions.

Limits per agent:

| Agent | SSE servers | `${NAME}` references |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | Written as SSE | Passed through |
| Codex | Left out with a warning (streamable HTTP only) | `Authorization: Bearer ${NAME}` becomes `bearer_token_env_var`. Any other header must be `${NAME}` alone, with `Bearer <token>` stored in the variable. An `env` entry cannot rename a variable (`API_KEY=${OTHER}` is left out); give the variable the name the server expects. |
| Antigravity | Left out with a warning (`stdio` and `http` only) | Not supported. `env` entries that are `${NAME}` are left out, so the server inherits the container's environment. Headers that contain `${NAME}` are left out with a warning. The next sync rewrites a server it manages, so add an authenticated server by hand under a name that `mcp.json` does not use ([agents](agents.md#mcp-servers-and-authentication)). |
| OpenCode | Written as a remote server, with a warning that this is not verified | Written as `{env:NAME}` |

Codex rewrites `config.toml` itself. `codex plugin add` puts its tables between the marker comments, and `codex mcp add` can remove the first marker. The Codex sync handles this as follows:

- It finds its own servers by the names recorded in `~/.agentainer/mcp-managed.json`. Only when that file lists no Codex servers, as in a config from an older Agentainer, does it take the servers between intact markers that `mcp.json` still lists.
- It keeps every other table and every comment, and writes its servers as a new marked block at the end.
- On its servers it owns the keys it can write: `command`, `args`, `env`, `env_vars`, `url`, `bearer_token_env_var`, `http_headers` and `env_http_headers`. If `config.toml` sets one of these on its server but `mcp.json` does not, the sync removes it and prints a warning. Put the value in `mcp.json` to keep it.
- Other keys you set on one of its servers, such as `enabled`, `enabled_tools` or `tools.<tool>.approval_mode` ([Codex config reference](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-reference)), stay with that server until you remove it from `mcp.json`.
- Before it writes, the sync parses the old and new file. If anything else would change, or `config.toml` is not valid TOML, it writes nothing, prints a warning and exits with status 1.

For Claude Code, Antigravity and OpenCode, a sync replaces the servers it manages, so settings you change inside one of those agents for such a server may not survive. If `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc` exists, the OpenCode sync stops with an error, because it edits only `opencode.json`.

Verified by hand: Codex and Antigravity listed a synced server's tools, and `claude mcp list` reported it as connected. Not verified: OpenCode, whose `opencode mcp list` prints "No MCP servers configured" even for a server that `opencode mcp add` wrote itself.

[Setting up the agents](agents.md#mcp-servers-and-authentication) covers each agent's own MCP login commands.

## Tools that agents install

`AGENTAINER_TOOLS` decides where `npm -g`, `cargo install`, `go install`, `uv tool` and `pipx` put things:

| Value | Location | Survives a new container |
|---|---|---|
| `ephemeral` (default) | `/var/lib/agentainer/tools` | No |
| `persist` | `~/.agentainer/tools` | Yes |

- Set it in the runtime env file before you create the container. Changing it does not change an existing container's environment.
- Image tools come first on `PATH`, so an installed tool never hides an image tool.
- `persist` keeps the installation roots on the home volume. It does not record the install commands or reproduce the same versions in another home, so keep those in your own setup notes or a custom image.
- It covers these user package managers only, not OS packages installed with `sudo apt`.
- When the image changes and persisted tools exist, the entrypoint warns on each start. `agentainer-tools reset` moves all persisted roots (Go, npm, cargo, uv, pipx and the Python user base) to a dated backup. Resets share a lock and reserve unique backup paths across containers.
- `agentainer-tools status` shows the effective mode, the selected root and the entries in `bin`, `npm/bin` and `python/bin`. It does not list every package or cache.
- `agentainer-extras` installs the optional tools the image pins (Kandev, OpenChamber, REA) into the same root ([Optional extras](extras.md)).

Ubuntu's Python refuses `pip install` outside a virtual environment, `pip install --user` included (PEP 668), so use `uv`, `pipx` or a venv. `PYTHONUSERBASE` points into the same tools root, but plain `pip` never installs there.

The image has `ansible-core` (`ansible`, `ansible-playbook`, `ansible-galaxy` and the other commands) without the community collections. Install the ones you use with `ansible-galaxy collection install community.general`. They go to `~/.ansible/collections` on the home volume.

Codex accepts only `wire_api = "responses"`, so the endpoint must serve the OpenAI Responses API ([Codex config reference](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-reference)).

## Startup messages

The entrypoint prints its messages on stderr, each starting with `agentainer:`. `AGENTAINER_QUIET=1` hides the line that lists which credential variables are set. Warnings and every other message still print.

If you do not set `AGENTAINER_QUIET`, the entrypoint sets it to `1` for a one-shot command, such as `podman run --rm IMAGE claude --version`, and to `0` for the default command, `sleep infinity`. Set `AGENTAINER_QUIET=0` to see the line for a one-shot command, or `AGENTAINER_QUIET=1` to hide it for a long-running container.
