## The launcher

[`bin/agentainer`](../bin/agentainer) wraps the `run` and `exec` commands below. It uses Podman when it finds it, otherwise Docker, and prints each command before it runs it.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `agentainer up [--name N] [--sudo] [--image I] [--publish MAPPING ...] [--] [DIR]` | Starts a detached container. DIR defaults to the current directory and becomes `/workspace`. |
| `agentainer attach [N]` | Runs `tmux new-session -A -s main` in the container |
| `agentainer shell [N]` | Opens a bash login shell |
| `agentainer start [N]` | Starts a stopped container, for example after the host or the Podman machine restarts |
| `agentainer update [N]` | Pulls the image the container was created from and recreates the container with the same options ([upgrading](#upgrading)) |
| `agentainer down [N]` | Removes a container carrying the Agentainer label. It refuses unrelated containers. The home volume stays. |
| `agentainer status` | Lists agentainer containers |
| `agentainer doctor [N] [--json]` | Runs offline diagnostics in the running container, without a TTY; see [diagnostic checks and exit codes](troubleshooting.md#offline-diagnostics). |

N defaults to `agentainer`. These variables override the launcher's defaults:

| Variable | Default |
|---|---|
| `AGENTAINER_IMAGE` | `ghcr.io/chadmayfield/agentainer:latest` |
| `AGENTAINER_ENV_FILE` | `~/.config/agentainer/env` |
| `AGENTAINER_HOME_VOLUME` | `agentainer-home` |
| `AGENTAINER_RUNTIME` | `podman` if installed, else `docker` |

For a host directory instead of the default named home volume, set `AGENTAINER_HOME_VOLUME` to an existing directory such as `"$HOME/.config/agentainer/home"`. Both mount at `/home/agent`. [Customizing Agentainer](customization.md) covers setup, your own dotfiles and separate test homes.

Home sources containing `/`, or exactly `.` or `..`, are host paths. Other values are named volumes. Use `./myhome` for a relative directory rather than `myhome`. The launcher warns if a mount exposes the host home, a parent of it, or the host root. Choose a project directory to limit access.

Limits:

- DIR must not contain `:`, because `-v` splits its value at `:`. Rename the directory to remove `:`.
- Container names also serve as hostnames. They must be at most 64 ASCII characters and start with a letter or digit ([launcher](../bin/agentainer), [hostname limit](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/sethostname.2.html)).
- `update` pulls from a registry, so it cannot update a container that runs an image you built locally (`localhost/...`). Use `agentainer down` and `agentainer up --image ...` for those.

### Locale and time zone

`up` passes your shell's locale and time zone into the new container with `-e`:

- `LANG` and `LC_ALL`.
- The locale categories glibc defines: `LC_CTYPE`, `LC_NUMERIC`, `LC_TIME`, `LC_COLLATE`, `LC_MONETARY`, `LC_MESSAGES`, `LC_PAPER`, `LC_NAME`, `LC_ADDRESS`, `LC_TELEPHONE`, `LC_MEASUREMENT` and `LC_IDENTIFICATION`. Other `LC_` names, such as iTerm2's `LC_TERMINAL`, stay on the host.
- `TZ`. When `TZ` is unset, the launcher reads the zone name from the `/etc/localtime` link, the part after `zoneinfo/`. On macOS that link is `/var/db/timezone/zoneinfo/America/Denver`, for example.

The launcher skips a value it cannot use:

- A locale must be `C.UTF-8`, `C.utf8`, or `language_TERRITORY.UTF-8` (or `.utf8`) with an optional `@modifier`, such as `en_US.UTF-8` or `sr_RS.UTF-8@latin`. Other codesets, and macOS's bare `LC_CTYPE=UTF-8`, are skipped, because tmux needs a UTF-8 locale.
- `TZ` must be a zone name such as `America/Denver` or `UTC`. A value that starts with `:` names a file and is skipped.

Variables your env file sets win. Both runtimes let `-e` override `--env-file` ([docker/cli `opts/parse.go`](https://github.com/docker/cli/blob/master/opts/parse.go), [Podman environment precedence](https://docs.podman.io/en/latest/markdown/podman-run.1.html)), so the launcher reads the variable names in the env file and does not pass those variables. It reads names only and never prints the file's values.

`up` records what it passed in the `io.github.chadmayfield.agentainer.locale` label. `update` passes those recorded values again and does not read your current shell, so an update from cron or SSH changes nothing. A container created before the label existed gets no locale or time zone from `update`. A value passed from your shell changes only when you run `agentainer down` and then `agentainer up`; the home volume stays. A `LANG` or `TZ` set in the env file is read again on every `update`, so editing it there takes effect on `update`.

## Development server ports

Repeat `--publish` or `-p` before DIR to publish development servers to the host:

```sh
bin/agentainer up --publish 3000:3000 --publish 8080:8000 "$HOME/code"
```

This maps host ports 3000 and 8080 to container ports 3000 and 8000. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8080` on the host for a server on container port 8000. The server must listen on the container's network interface, for example `0.0.0.0`, not only on its own loopback address ([Docker publishing](https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/port-publishing/), [Podman publishing](https://docs.podman.io/en/latest/markdown/podman-run.1.html)).

Each mapping is `[IPv4:]HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT[/tcp|udp]`:

| Form | Example | Result |
|---|---|---|
| No address | `--publish 3000:3000` | Binds `127.0.0.1` on the host, TCP |
| UDP | `--publish 5353:5353/udp` | UDP instead of TCP |
| Explicit address | `--publish 0.0.0.0:3000:3000` | Binds all host IPv4 interfaces |
| Joined forms | `--publish=3000:3000`, `-p3000:3000` | Accepted |
| IPv6, port ranges, automatic host ports | | Not supported; use a direct runtime command |

The [optional extras](extras.md) Kandev and OpenChamber are web apps that need a published port:

```sh
# Kandev
bin/agentainer up --publish 38429:38429 "$HOME/code"
kandev --port 38429 --headless                       # inside the container
# OpenChamber
bin/agentainer up --publish 3000:3000 "$HOME/code"
openchamber --lan --port 3000 --ui-password '<password>'   # inside the container
```

Kandev's local mode is not an authenticated multi-user boundary, and OpenChamber needs `--ui-password` to protect browser access, so keep the default `127.0.0.1` host binding ([Kandev](extras.md#kandev), [OpenChamber](extras.md#openchamber)).

Ports must be 1 through 65535. For a remote engine, the bind address belongs to the engine host. With a local VM, reachability also depends on the runtime's port forwarding.

The launcher validates mappings before it creates a container and before it pulls an update. With no `--publish` option, it publishes no ports. `update` keeps the recorded mappings. Containers created by older launchers without a ports label publish no ports. To change the mappings, recreate the container with new `up` options; the home stays.

## Without the launcher

Use a published version tag. The registry has no `latest` manifest until a stable release publishes it ([release policy](versions.md#releases)).

```sh
docker run -d --name agentainer --hostname agentainer \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges=true \
  --sysctl "net.ipv4.ping_group_range=1000 1000" \
  -v agentainer-home:/home/agent \
  -v "$HOME/code:/workspace" -w /workspace \
  --env-file "$HOME/.config/agentainer/env" \
  ghcr.io/chadmayfield/agentainer:0.1.0-dev.20261024.1
docker exec -it agentainer tmux new-session -A -s main
```

With Podman, use the same commands and add `--userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000`. It maps your host user to the container user, so files in `/workspace` stay yours (`man podman-run`).

- The container runs `sleep infinity` under `tini` as PID 1. Sessions are `exec` calls into tmux, so agents keep running when a terminal or SSH connection drops.
- The whole home directory `/home/agent` is one volume. Logins, settings and `AGENTS.md` live there and survive a new container. Containers that use the same volume share logins, and two containers running the same agent write the same files.
- The `ping_group_range` sysctl lets `ping` work without the `NET_RAW` capability. It names only GID 1000: with Podman's keep-id the GID map is not contiguous, and a wider range breaks.

## Container health

The image runs [`agentainer-healthcheck`](../rootfs/usr/local/bin/agentainer-healthcheck) through the [Dockerfile `HEALTHCHECK` instruction](https://docs.docker.com/reference/dockerfile/#healthcheck):

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Interval | 30 seconds |
| Timeout | 5 seconds |
| Start period | 180 seconds |
| Retries before `unhealthy` | 3 |

The probe checks the entrypoint's completion marker, read, write and search access to the home directory, and that the active tools symlink points to a readable, searchable directory. Startup clears the marker, including after a restart. The probe reads no agent settings or credentials, runs no agents, changes no home files and makes no network requests. It does not check free disk space or whether each tool works. [`agentainer doctor`](troubleshooting.md#offline-diagnostics) checks configuration syntax and that tools start; neither checks free space, so use `df -h` for that.

Inspect the status and recent probe results from the host:

```sh
podman inspect --format '{{json .State.Health}}' agentainer
docker inspect --format '{{json .State.Health}}' agentainer
```

Health status reports readiness. It does not restart the container. Kubernetes ignores image health checks; configure pod probes separately ([Kubernetes probes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/)).

Podman inherits an image health check only from a Docker-format manifest ([Podman source](https://github.com/containers/podman/blob/v5.3.2/pkg/specgen/generate/container.go#L67-L87)). `scripts/build.sh` builds Docker format with both engines. Release images are OCI manifests with SBOM and provenance attestations, so a raw `podman run` of a release image needs the probe passed explicitly:

```sh
--health-cmd=/usr/local/bin/agentainer-healthcheck --health-interval=30s \
--health-timeout=5s --health-start-period=180s --health-retries=3
```

The launcher does not add these options ([Podman options](https://docs.podman.io/en/v5.3.2/markdown/podman-run.1.html#health-cmd-command)). Older images without the probe need an image update and a new container. [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#common-problems) covers Podman-specific health states.

## sudo

The image has passwordless sudo, and `--security-opt no-new-privileges=true` turns it off ([Docker reference](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/)). `agentainer up --sudo` leaves that option out.

With sudo on, an agent can change anything in the container, including the agent binaries and the settings that stop them from updating themselves. Packages installed with `sudo apt install` are gone when the container is recreated. Under rootful Docker, container root is UID 0 on the host, limited by the container's namespaces.

## File ownership

- Rootless Podman with keep-id: files in `/workspace` belong to your host user.
- Rootful Docker on Linux: files written to `/workspace` belong to UID 1000 on the host. If your UID is different, use Podman or rootless Docker, or build an image with your UID and GID.

`scripts/build.sh` uses Podman unless `RUNTIME` says otherwise. On a Docker host:

```sh
RUNTIME=docker sh scripts/build.sh --uid "$(id -u)" --gid "$(id -g)"
```

With a GID other than 1000, also set `--sysctl "net.ipv4.ping_group_range=<gid> <gid>"` in your `run` command, or `ping` fails. The launcher always passes `1000 1000`.

`sh tests/host/test-build-uid.sh` builds an image with `--uid 1001 --gid 20` and checks the agent user. When the build fails, it prints the last 80 lines of the build output.

## Other options

- SSH agent on a Linux host: add `-v "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK:/run/ssh-agent.sock" -e SSH_AUTH_SOCK=/run/ssh-agent.sock`. A forwarded agent lets container processes request signatures with its loaded keys, so use a dedicated agent holding only the keys this session needs ([credential exposure](security.md#what-the-container-isolates)). `ssh-agent` refuses a client whose UID differs from its own unless the client is root (`uid mismatch` in [ssh-agent.c](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/master/ssh-agent.c)), so the container user needs the UID of the user who started the agent:
  - Rootless Podman with keep-id, as the launcher runs it, maps your host UID to the container user ([podman-run](https://docs.podman.io/en/latest/markdown/podman-run.1.html)). Not verified with an SSH agent.
  - Rootful Docker runs the container user as UID 1000. If your UID is different, build your own image as described in [File ownership](#file-ownership).

  Verified in CI with rootful Docker on Linux only, in a narrow check: CI makes the socket's directory readable, then runs `ssh-add -l` as the entrypoint with `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"`, so the normal entrypoint does not run. Not verified: macOS, where the socket path depends on the runtime. For git, the default is `GH_TOKEN` ([logins](logins.md)).
- SELinux hosts may need `:z` on volume mounts. Not verified.

## Upgrading

```sh
bin/agentainer update
```

`update` pulls the image the container was created from and recreates the container; the home volume stays. Without the launcher, pull first: a plain `run` does not pull a newer image for a tag that is already on your machine. For Kubernetes, see [docs/kubernetes.md](kubernetes.md#upgrading-and-removing).

How `update` works:

- `up` records DIR, image, sudo setting, home volume, published ports, the env file's absolute path and the [locale and time zone](#locale-and-time-zone) it passed as container labels. `update` reads them back.
- `update` changes nothing when the pull fails, when DIR or the env file no longer exists, or when the container has no option labels.
- After the pull, `update` renames the old container to `cx-agentainer-backup-N` and stops it. It removes the backup only after the new container starts. If creation or startup fails, it restores the old container in its previous running or stopped state. Changes the new container made to the home or workspace are not rolled back.
- Startup may take up to 180 seconds. The new container counts as started when the entrypoint's completion marker exists; for an older image without the marker, when its tools link exists. If the launcher is killed before it can restore a failed update, inspect `cx-agentainer-backup-N` before you retry. `update` refuses to overwrite an existing backup.
- A successful `update` leaves the new container running, even when the old one was stopped.
- `AGENTAINER_DRY_RUN=1` prints the commands that change state instead of running them. `update` and `down` still run read-only `inspect` calls to read the recorded options.

On the first start of the new image, the entrypoint adds files that are missing from your home volume. It does not replace your files with the image's copies, with these exceptions. Each exception changes only the part the entrypoint manages:

| File | What changes | When |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.agentainer/AGENTS.md` | Replaced with the new default | You never edited it and the image's version allows it; [AGENTS.md](configuration.md#agentsmd) lists the conditions |
| Agent MCP configs | Servers that `agentainer-mcp sync` added | `~/.agentainer/mcp.json` changed, or you run `agentainer-mcp sync` ([MCP servers](configuration.md#mcp-servers)) |
| `~/.gitconfig` | The GitHub credential helper, from `gh auth setup-git` | `GH_TOKEN` or `GITHUB_TOKEN` is set and this container's `gh` is not already the helper ([GitHub and Git](logins.md#github-and-git)) |
| `~/.gitconfig` | `user.name` or `user.email` | `GIT_AUTHOR_NAME` or `GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL` is set and the file has no value for it |
| `~/.config/opencode/service.json` | Created by `opencode service set disabled true` | The file does not exist yet |

Everything else:

- Logins, agent settings and history stay.
- New defaults in the image's seed files do not reach an existing home. Compare yours with the image's copies in `/etc/agentainer/home/`, for example `.claude/settings.json` and `.codex/config.toml`.
- With `AGENTAINER_TOOLS=persist`, tools you installed stay on `PATH` after the image's own tools ([tools that agents install](configuration.md#tools-that-agents-install)).
- MCP servers sync again only when `~/.agentainer/mcp.json` changes. Run `agentainer-mcp sync` to sync after an upgrade.
- Anything installed with `sudo apt install` is gone, as after every new container.

## What the container isolates

The container restricts direct filesystem and process access through its mounts and namespaces. Writable mounts, shared home files and reachable host services can let container code affect the host.

It does not isolate:

- The code you mount. Agents can change or delete it.
- Host execution of mounted files. Git configuration and hooks, generated executables, editor tasks and project scripts can run as your host user after an agent changes them. Review these files before running host commands, or use a separate host clone. Disabling Git hooks alone does not disable every execution path ([Git configuration](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config)).
- Host network services. Whether container code can reach a service bound to host loopback depends on the runtime's networking; Podman, for example, provides `host.containers.internal` ([Podman networking](https://docs.podman.io/en/latest/markdown/podman-run.1.html)). Authenticate sensitive host services, and use an offline network when network access is unnecessary.
- Shared home volumes. Every container using the same home trusts its shell startup files, agent settings and installed tools. Use different homes for different trust levels. Enabling sudo in a later container also grants its startup code access to container root.
- Forwarded SSH agents. Processes with access to the socket can request signatures with its loaded keys. Use a dedicated agent with only the required keys. Keys with confirmation constraints can require host approval ([ssh-add](https://man.openbsd.org/ssh-add)).
- Terminal output. Shells and attached panes send output to your host terminal. Arbitrary tmux passthrough is disabled by default. Enabling `allow-passthrough` in your own tmux configuration permits wrapped escape sequences to reach the outer terminal, including clipboard requests on terminals that accept them ([tmux manual](https://man.openbsd.org/tmux)).
- Outbound network access, unless you use the NetworkPolicy in Kubernetes ([docs/kubernetes.md](kubernetes.md#network-policy)).
- Credentials. See [credentials and runtime settings](#credentials-and-runtime-settings).
- The host kernel. This is a container, not a VM.
- Everything inside the container once sudo is on ([sudo](running.md#sudo)).

The image runs as the non-root user `agent` (UID 1000), and agent binaries are root-owned. With sudo off, agents cannot replace them. A raw image run has passwordless sudo unless the runtime sets `no-new-privileges`. The launcher sets it by default, and the Kubernetes example disables privilege escalation. Add the option to raw runs too ([sudo](running.md#sudo)).

### Credentials and runtime settings

- **Every variable in the env file or Secret is readable by every process in the container**: all four agents, the tools they run, and MCP servers. Pass only the keys you need, and prefer narrowly scoped tokens.
- Env-file values stay in the engine's stored container configuration. Users with engine access can read them with `inspect`; on rootful Docker that includes members of the Docker group ([Podman inspect](https://docs.podman.io/en/latest/markdown/podman-inspect.1.html), [Docker env files](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/#env)).
- Changing the env file does not update an existing container, and stop and start do not refresh it. Recreate the container with `agentainer update` or `down` and `up`, and inspect leftover update backups before you remove them.
- Agent update variables and `GOTOOLCHAIN=local` are defaults that container code can override. Root ownership is what stops ordinary replacement of image tools; sudo removes that protection. Go details are in [language tooling](language-tooling.md#go-with-gopls) ([Go toolchains](https://go.dev/doc/toolchain)).

## Agent permissions

Agents keep their own approval prompts; the image turns on no skip-permissions mode. If you turn one on, note Anthropic's warning: "When executed with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, dev containers do not prevent a malicious project from exfiltrating anything accessible inside the container, including the Claude Code credentials" ([devcontainer docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/devcontainer)).

Codex's own sandbox is off: the seeded `~/.codex/config.toml` sets `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"`, so the container provides the isolation. The file's comment gives the reason: Codex's bubblewrap sandbox cannot start inside a container ("bwrap: Can't mount devpts on /newroot/dev/pts: Permission denied"). Whether it starts under every runtime configuration is not verified. The seeded `approval_policy = "on-request"` lets Codex ask for approval; it does not require confirmation for every command. Codex can run commands against mounted files and use available network access without prompting. Treat every writable mount and supplied credential as accessible to it ([OpenAI approval semantics](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-approvals-security)).

Antigravity's terms say: "Wrapping `agy` inside third-party coding agents or applications ... is not supported under consumer plans" ([Antigravity FAQ](https://antigravity.google/docs/faq.md)). Agentainer installs `agy` for you to run yourself and does not wrap it.

Gemini CLI is not included. Google wrote: "On June 18, 2026, Gemini CLI and Gemini Code Assist IDE extensions will stop serving requests for Google AI Pro and Ultra, as well as those using it free of charge using Gemini Code Assist for individuals" ([Google Developers Blog](https://developers.googleblog.com/an-important-update-transitioning-gemini-cli-to-antigravity-cli/)). Antigravity CLI is Google's named replacement.

## Vulnerability reports

CI scans candidate images and the exact pushed release digests with an independent Trivy container pinned by digest in `versions.env`. It does not execute the scanner bundled in the image under test or load a secret-rule override from the checkout. A secret fails the build or stops release promotion. Vulnerabilities are reported and do not fail it ([workflow](../.github/workflows/build.yml), [Trivy image scans](https://trivy.dev/docs/latest/target/container_image/)).

- Pull requests and `develop`: the run's summary page shows counts by severity, how many have a fix, and up to 50 critical findings. The full trivy JSON is the `vulnerabilities-<arch>` artifact on that run.
- Releases: the scan runs on the images pushed to GHCR. The release notes start with the same summary, and `vulnerabilities-amd64.json` and `vulnerabilities-arm64.json` are attached to the release.
- Kernel CVEs filed against `linux-libc-dev`, the kernel header package that C compilers need, are counted separately: the container runs on the host's kernel.

Many findings sit in upstream binaries that this repo installs as released. They are fixed by upstream releases, which reach the image through the scheduled version update ([docs/versions.md](versions.md)). [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md#vulnerabilities-in-bundled-tools) describes how a tool that stops shipping fixes is handled.

## Offline diagnostics

From the host, check the running container with:

```sh
bin/agentainer doctor
bin/agentainer doctor agentainer-test --json
```

N defaults to `agentainer`. Inside the container, run `agentainer-doctor` or `agentainer-doctor --json`. The image must include that command; updating only the host launcher does not add it to an older image.

The command reports `ok`, `warn` or `fail` for:

- The image's `/etc/agentainer/versions.json` inventory format.
- Home-directory read, write and search access, plus group/other write permissions.
- The tools mode, active symlink target and tool-root write access.
- Syntax of the five seeded agent settings files listed in [default configuration](defaults.md#agent-configurations).
- Shared MCP input validation, ownership metadata, interrupted writes and the last successful input-hash stamp. An active sync produces a warning instead of reading partially updated state.
- Version-command execution for the four agents and the core tools listed in [`agentainer-doctor`](../rootfs/usr/local/bin/agentainer-doctor).

Settings checks respect `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` ([Claude settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings#find-or-create-your-settings-files)), `CODEX_HOME` ([Codex configuration](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-reference)) and `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` for OpenCode (`opencode debug paths` shows the resolved paths). Missing settings files and OpenCode JSONC files produce warnings; invalid JSON or TOML and unreadable files fail. The check covers home settings syntax, not the precedence of project, profile and managed settings.

Version probes run in a temporary directory with a temporary home, without credentials, with a five-second timeout each. The report prints no configuration values, provider URLs, tool output or exception details. The command does not rewrite settings, install tools, repair MCP state or make model requests.

Exit status is `0` when no check failed, `1` when any check failed, and `2` for invalid arguments. Warnings do not fail the command. JSON output contains an overall `status` and a `checks` array; each check has `name`, `status` and `message` fields.

Not checked: login validity, agent-specific setting semantics, model access, MCP server connectivity and live approval behavior. MCP status records the last successful sync input, not whether every server is available. When the syntax checks pass but an agent still rejects a setting, use that agent's own diagnostics ([setting up the agents](agents.md#check-the-setup)).

## Common problems

**The container reports `starting` or `unhealthy`.**
Inspect `.State.Health` as described in [container health](running.md#container-health). A new container can stay `starting` while its entrypoint runs. Failures report `startup incomplete`, `home permissions` or `tools directory unavailable`, without printing environment values. Check the container's startup logs and home mount permissions, then run `agentainer doctor`. A repaired container becomes `healthy` on its next successful probe. The probe does not test agent authentication or network access.

**Podman shows `starting` with no probe log.**
An older image without a health check can show `starting` on Podman 5.3.2 with an empty `.Config.Healthcheck` object. That empty object is not a running check. Podman sets `starting` whenever a non-null health-check object exists ([Podman source](https://github.com/containers/podman/blob/v5.3.2/libpod/container_internal.go#L1291-L1300)). Podman 5.3.2 also keeps suppressing failure counts until the start period ends, while Docker ends it after the first successful probe ([Podman source](https://github.com/containers/podman/blob/v5.3.2/libpod/healthcheck.go#L127-L136)).

**A Podman container has no health check although the image defines one.**
Add `--health-cmd=/usr/local/bin/agentainer-healthcheck` and the other options from [container health](running.md#container-health) to a raw `podman run`, only with an image that includes the probe. The launcher does not add them ([Podman health command option](https://docs.podman.io/en/v5.3.2/markdown/podman-run.1.html#health-cmd-command)).

**`sudo: The "no new privileges" flag is set, which prevents sudo from running as root.`**
sudo is off by default. Remove the container with `bin/agentainer down` (the home stays), then run `bin/agentainer up --sudo` with the same DIR. For a raw `docker run` or `podman run`, leave out `--security-opt no-new-privileges=true` ([sudo](running.md#sudo)).

**`ping: socket: Operation not permitted`**
The container was started without `--sysctl "net.ipv4.ping_group_range=1000 1000"`. The launcher and the Kubernetes example set it; add it to raw `run` commands.

**The container name `agentainer` is already in use**
A container with that name exists. If it is running, `bin/agentainer attach` connects to it. If it is stopped, `bin/agentainer start` starts it, and `bin/agentainer down` removes it. The home volume stays either way.

**`agentainer: ... has no option labels` when running `agentainer update`**
`update` needs the option labels that `agentainer up` records, so it cannot recreate this container. The fix depends on the container's labels:

- It has the Agentainer label but no option labels, for example from an older launcher: run `bin/agentainer down`, then `bin/agentainer up` with the options you want.
- It has no Agentainer label, for example from a raw `docker run` or `podman run`: `down` refuses it with `refusing to remove ... because it has no agentainer label`. Record its mounts and options with `docker inspect` or `podman inspect`, remove it with `docker rm` or `podman rm`, then create it with `bin/agentainer up`, using the same home volume and DIR.

**Files in `/workspace` belong to UID 1000 on a Linux host.**
That is rootful Docker with a host UID other than 1000. Build an image with your UID, or use Podman or rootless Docker ([file ownership](running.md#file-ownership)).

**An agent shows an old setting after an upgrade.**
The entrypoint adds the image's files only where your home volume has none, so new default settings in the image do not replace yours. Compare your files with the image's copies in `/etc/agentainer/home/`. [Upgrading](running.md#upgrading) lists the few files the entrypoint does change.

**`claude doctor` warns that `~/.local/bin` is not in `PATH` and says to run `claude install`.**
The image installs Claude Code at `/usr/local/bin/claude`, and a new image brings a new version. The warnings look for Anthropic's per-user install in `~/.local`, which the image does not use. Ignore them: `claude install` prints "Updates are disabled by your administrator" and changes nothing.

**`agentainer-mcp` warns that an agent "already has a server named ... that agentainer did not add".**
That agent's own config has a server with the same name, which the sync leaves alone. Rename one of them in `~/.agentainer/mcp.json` or in the agent.

**The tmux session does not start over SSH in Kubernetes: "open terminal failed: terminal does not support clear".**
tmux needs `TERM`. The webhook in `deploy/kubernetes` sets it; check that ContainerSSH uses that webhook's `/config` answer ([docs/kubernetes.md](kubernetes.md#logging-in)).

## Pinned inputs

[`versions.env`](../versions.env) pins every input of the main image (`Containerfile`): the base image digest, the apt snapshot date, each agent and tool version, and the checksum of every download. The build checks each download against it. The one exception is the Rust toolchain: `rustup-init` downloads the components and checks each against the hashes in Rust's own channel manifest. The [Kelos variant](kelos.md#pins) keeps its pins in `Containerfile.kelos`.

Node.js is the official Linux tarball from nodejs.org, installed in `/opt/node` with `node`, `npm` and `npx` linked into `/usr/local/bin`. `versions.env` pins `NODE_VERSION` and the two Linux checksums (`NODE_SHA256_AMD64`, `NODE_SHA256_ARM64`), and the scheduled update follows the 26.x line. The image removes `include/`, `share/`, `README.md` and `CHANGELOG.md` from the install. Verification happens in two places: the updater checks the GPG signature on Node.js's checksum list before it writes the pins ([Node.js release keyring](#nodejs-release-keyring)), and the build checks the downloaded tarball against the pinned SHA-256 (`build/install-tool.sh`).

Claude Code is the native binary from Anthropic's release host, the file Anthropic's native installer downloads. The scheduled update checks the release's `manifest.json` against Anthropic's GPG signature before it pins the binary's SHA-256 ([binary integrity](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup#binary-integrity-and-code-signing)).

gosec, gitleaks and the ContainerSSH guest agent (`containerssh-agent`) are upstream release archives. The build checks each against the SHA-256 in the project's published `*_checksums.txt` (`GOSEC_`, `GITLEAKS_` and `CONTAINERSSH_AGENT_` pins). The image installs the agent at `/usr/local/bin/containerssh-agent` and links it at `/usr/bin/containerssh-agent`, ContainerSSH's default `agentPath` ([`AgentPath` default in `config/kubernetes.go` at ContainerSSH v0.6.0](https://github.com/ContainerSSH/ContainerSSH/blob/v0.6.0/config/kubernetes.go#L113)). The updater takes these three tools' hashes only from the release's `gosec_<version>_checksums.txt`, `gitleaks_<version>_checksums.txt` and `agent_<version>_checksums.txt`, and refuses a release that lacks the file.

The agent version follows the ContainerSSH server image. `CONTAINERSSH_AGENT_SERIES` in `scripts/bump_versions.py` maps the server's tag series (`v0.6`) to the agent minor series tested with it (`0.11`), and the updater only proposes newer patch releases in that series. If the server tag has no entry, the updater keeps the current agent pin and prints why. The `v0.6` tag's digest can move between patch releases, so a mapping change needs a review of the verified pair of server digest and agent version. The verified pair is the server `docker.io/containerssh/containerssh:v0.6@sha256:f6b195c221739b0f1a43c567bc9df0a0f3b3bd92ccc25ef451e6d4122820c13b` (`CONTAINERSSH_IMAGE`) with `containerssh-agent` 0.11.0 (`CONTAINERSSH_AGENT_VERSION`). On 2026-11-04 SFTP, `ssh -L` and `ssh -D` worked with this pair in a cluster, in persistent mode with `disableAgent: true`. `VERIFIED_CONTAINERSSH_PAIR` in `scripts/bump_versions.py` records this pair, and `test_pinned_containerssh_pair_is_the_cluster_verified_pair` fails when `versions.env` pins a different server image reference (name, tag or digest) or agent version. A pull request from the scheduled update that changes either pin therefore fails CI until someone re-runs the SFTP, `ssh -L` and `ssh -D` check from [docs/kubernetes.md](kubernetes.md#sftp-and-port-forwarding) against the new pair and updates the constant and this paragraph. Do not merge a guest agent or server update before that check. The test runs in the `build` workflow on the pull request, not in the bump job, so the pull request still opens and shows the failure. That day Docker Hub's `v0.6` tag resolved to this digest, `v0.6.1` resolved to a different digest, and no `v0.6.0` tag existed.

Each tool is built in its own stage, so an update downloads only the layers that changed:

| Condition | Effect on layer digests |
|---|---|
| Release build, tool unchanged, same BuildKit (`BUILDKIT_IMAGE`) | Byte-identical to the previous release's layer. File times later than `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` are set to it (BuildKit's `rewrite-timestamp` option). |
| Release that updates BuildKit | Every layer's digest can change |
| `scripts/build.sh` with Podman 5.6 or later | Same as a release build |
| `scripts/build.sh` with an older Podman server | The script leaves the options out and prints a warning. The image works the same, but every layer gets a new digest. |

`/etc/agentainer/versions.json` in the image lists every pin and every installed apt package version, and an `apt_source` field that says where apt got them.

### apt snapshot and the archive fallback

`APT_SNAPSHOT` pins every apt package to one day of `snapshot.ubuntu.com`. When that service fails, a build made through `scripts/build.sh` falls back to `archive.ubuntu.com` as it is that day, so a build does not stop on someone else's outage. Every build in `build.yml` except the release `publish` job goes through that script: pull request builds, pushes to `develop` and `main`, and local builds. The `publish` job builds with `docker/build-push-action` from the `versions.env` pins and never falls back.

A fallback build records itself in three places:

- `/usr/local/share/agentainer/apt-source` holds one line, `archive-fallback <UTC date> (snapshot <APT_SNAPSHOT> unavailable)`. A snapshot build holds `snapshot <APT_SNAPSHOT>`.
- `/etc/agentainer/versions.json` has the same line in `apt_source`.
- The build report in the job summary prints a `WARNING` line, and the image job adds a warning annotation to the run.

A fallback image is not reproducible and cannot be released. Two checks keep a fallback from reaching a release:

- `scripts/check-release-platform.sh` fails the `publish` job unless the pushed image's `apt-source` is exactly `snapshot <APT_SNAPSHOT>` with the pin from `versions.env`.
- `scripts/check-apt-fallback.sh` fails the image job when the build fell back and the change modifies `APT_SNAPSHOT` in `versions.env` or `build/apt-packages.txt`, because a release would install those inputs from the snapshot and the fallback build did not test them. A fallback with other changes only warns. Without a base commit to compare with (a manual run, for example), it only warns.

For a local build, the fallback is the default. To make a build fail when the snapshot is unavailable, run `scripts/build.sh --strict-apt` or set `APT_FALLBACK=` (empty) in the environment. The `Containerfile` enables the fallback only for the value `archive`. [`build/apt-install.sh`](../build/apt-install.sh) does the install.

The engine caches the apt layer. After a fallback build, a later default local build can reuse that layer even when the snapshot works again, and the image keeps recording the fallback. `build.sh` prints a warning in that case. To try the snapshot again, run `scripts/build.sh --no-cache`, which passes `--no-cache` to the engine's `build` (`podman build --help` and `docker build --help` list it), or run `--strict-apt`, whose build argument differs and so misses the cached layer.

`versions.env` also pins the [optional extras](extras.md), which the image carries as lockfiles but does not install ([Optional extras](#optional-extras)).

## Scheduled updates

On the 1st and 15th of each month at 06:00 UTC, [`.github/workflows/bump.yml`](../.github/workflows/bump.yml) resolves the newest upstream versions with [`scripts/bump_versions.py`](../scripts/bump_versions.py) and opens a pull request against `develop`. It refuses to write any value that does not match the expected format for its pin. The pull request's build page shows which pins changed. A maintainer reviews and merges it by hand, and nothing is published until the next release.

An update PR lists increases to the leading number of a three-part tool version under "Major-version upgrades" and asks the maintainer to acknowledge the compatibility review in its description. CI does not enforce that checkbox. Minor updates to tools below 1.0 can also break compatibility, so review their upstream notes as well ([Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/)).

The resolver follows current upstream release pointers with no minimum release age, except for the optional extras ([Optional extras](#optional-extras)). Proposed binaries run in build and test jobs before anyone reviews the pull request. Checksums and publisher signatures establish byte identity and the signing identity, not that the code is safe, so review upstream changes before merging.

Run the same workflow manually through its `workflow_dispatch` trigger for an urgent security fix or an upstream change that breaks an agent. GitHub documents [scheduled](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule) and [manual](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#workflow_dispatch) triggers.

The workflow opens the pull request with a GitHub App token when the repository has both the variable `BUMP_APP_CLIENT_ID` and the secret `BUMP_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`; CI then starts on its own. Otherwise it uses `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and GitHub holds the pull request's CI until a maintainer chooses "Approve workflows to run" ([CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md#the-bump-github-app) describes the App).

## Releases

Releases use [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/):

- Stable versions have the form `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, such as `0.1.0`.
- Development prereleases use the next intended version followed by `-dev.YYYYMMDD.N`, such as `0.1.0-dev.20261019.1`. The date must exist, and the build number starts at 1 and increments for another build that day.
- The parser also accepts other SemVer prerelease identifiers, such as `0.1.0-rc.1`.
- Container tags exclude SemVer build metadata (`+...`) and are limited to 128 characters ([distribution tag format](https://github.com/distribution/reference/blob/main/regexp.go)).

Versions below `1.0.0` are initial development, without a stable compatibility promise. Agentainer's public interfaces are its launcher commands, documented environment variables, configuration paths and persistent-home upgrade behavior. Bundled tool versions remain separate in `versions.env`.

Each release publishes `ghcr.io/chadmayfield/agentainer` for amd64 and arm64:

- tagged with the version and `sha-<commit>`, with `latest` reserved for stable releases;
- signed with cosign keyless signing, the index and each architecture's image;
- with an SBOM and BuildKit provenance for each architecture, a signed GitHub provenance attestation for the multi-architecture index, and zstd-compressed layers.

A release requires a maintainer-signed tag on a release merge in `main`; a branch merge alone does not publish. [CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md#releases) describes the release procedure, the checks before publication and how `latest` moves.

Pull an explicit version tag. Prereleases never move `latest`, so before the first stable release there is no `latest` tag:

```sh
podman pull ghcr.io/chadmayfield/agentainer:0.1.0-dev.20261024.1
AGENTAINER_IMAGE=ghcr.io/chadmayfield/agentainer:0.1.0-dev.20261024.1 bin/agentainer up
```

A version exists only after its release workflow completes. A merge to `develop` runs CI and does not publish an image. To use features merged after the newest release tag, build the image locally with `scripts/build.sh`.

A runtime needs zstd support to pull the image:

| Runtime | First version that pulls zstd layers |
|---|---|
| Docker Engine | 23.0.0 ("Add support for pulling `zstd` compressed layers", [Engine 23.0 release notes](https://docs.docker.com/engine/release-notes/23.0/), moby/moby#41759) |
| containerd, including Kubernetes nodes that use it | 1.5.0 ("Add support for layers compressed with zstd", [containerd v1.5.0 release notes](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/releases/tag/v1.5.0)) |
| Podman | Not verified. Podman's release notes do not name a version. containers/image added zstd in containers/image#639, and Podman 1.6.2 is the first release whose `go.mod` uses a containers/image version with that change. |

The [release workflow for `v0.1.0-dev.20261019.1`](https://github.com/chadmayfield/agentainer/actions/runs/39373669375) completed signing, attestation storage and registry verification. Each later release must pass the same checks for its own digest.

## Verifying a release before use

Use a trusted checkout of this repository and independently installed Docker Buildx, cosign and GitHub CLI. Verify the maintainer-signed release tag with the trusted public key and fingerprint first. Obtain the full source commit from that tag and the image index digest from the registry. Review the digest before running the verifier; never substitute an unverified mutable tag afterward.

```sh
set -eu
version=0.1.0-dev.20261024.1
git verify-tag "v$version"
commit=$(git rev-parse "v$version^{commit}")
# Replace this placeholder with the release's full index digest.
digest=sha256:REPLACE_WITH_64_HEX_DIGITS
python3 tests/host/test-published-image.py ghcr.io/chadmayfield/agentainer "$digest" \
  "https://github.com/chadmayfield/agentainer/.github/workflows/build.yml@refs/tags/v$version" \
  https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com chadmayfield/agentainer "$commit" "refs/tags/v$version"
AGENTAINER_IMAGE="ghcr.io/chadmayfield/agentainer@$digest" bin/agentainer up
```

The verifier checks:

- Index and platform signatures against the exact workflow identity for the release tag and the GitHub OIDC issuer ([Sigstore CI verification](https://docs.sigstore.dev/quickstart/quickstart-ci/)).
- GitHub provenance against the repository, source commit, tag ref and workflow identity, rejecting self-hosted runners ([GitHub verification flags](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_attestation_verify)).
- Both platforms' BuildKit provenance against the expected source repository and commit. A dirty or different revision fails ([BuildKit provenance fields](https://docs.docker.com/build/metadata/attestations/slsa-provenance/)).
- SBOM and provenance descriptors bound to each platform manifest, then a pull and native startup by the verified index digest ([attestation storage](https://docs.docker.com/build/metadata/attestations/attestation-storage/)).

It pulls and starts the verified digest, so run it only where you intend to run that release. It needs registry access and GitHub authentication. It does not establish a SLSA level or validate every SBOM package entry. Its commands and flags are in the [verifier source](../tests/host/test-published-image.py). The launcher does not perform these checks.

## Upstream publisher verification

The updater requires `gh`, `cosign` and GnuPG in addition to Python. The scheduled workflow installs cosign through its pinned installer action. [`scripts/verify_upstream.py`](../scripts/verify_upstream.py) checks supported publishers before the resolver writes any pins. A missing verification tool, missing signing asset, changed checksum or failed signature stops the update. Build downloads still check their pinned hashes. The optional extras are the exception: a failed check keeps only that extra's pin ([Optional extras](#optional-extras)).

| Download | Required publisher check |
|---|---|
| GitHub CLI | GitHub provenance from `cli/cli`, workflow `deployment.yml` on `refs/heads/trunk`. |
| uv | GitHub provenance from `astral-sh/uv`, workflow `release.yml` on `refs/heads/main`. |
| Ruff | GitHub provenance from `astral-sh/ruff`, workflow `release.yml` on `refs/heads/main`. |
| golangci-lint | GitHub provenance from `golangci/golangci-lint`, workflow `release.yml` at the selected release tag. |
| yq | Signed BSD checksum list from `mikefarah/yq`, workflow `release.yml` at the selected release tag. |
| Trivy binary | Signed checksum list from `aquasecurity/trivy`, workflow `reusable-release.yaml` at the selected release tag. |
| Codex package | Sigstore bundle for the whole package from `openai/codex`, workflow `rust-release.yml` at the selected release tag. |
| Claude Code | GPG-signed release manifest with the pinned Anthropic key fingerprint. |
| Node.js | GPG-signed `SHASUMS256.txt` by one of the release keys in `scripts/keys/nodejs-release-keys.asc`. |
| AWS CLI | GPG signature (`<zip>.sig`) on each installer zip, by the AWS CLI Team key in `scripts/keys/aws-cli-public-key.asc` with the fingerprint pinned in the updater. AWS publishes no checksums, so the updater computes the SHA-256 pins from the verified zips. |
| Optional extras (npm) | npm registry signature on every lockfile entry, by a key in `scripts/keys/npm-registry-keys.json` ([Optional extras](#optional-extras)). |
| gosec | Checksum verified; publisher signature not verified. The SHA-256 comes from `gosec_<version>_checksums.txt`. |
| gitleaks | Checksum verified; publisher signature not verified. The SHA-256 comes from `gitleaks_<version>_checksums.txt`. |
| ContainerSSH guest agent | Checksum verified; publisher signature not verified. The SHA-256 comes from `agent_<version>_checksums.txt`. |

GitHub provenance checks require the exact workflow certificate identity, repository, source ref and GitHub OIDC issuer ([GitHub CLI verification](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_attestation_verify), [CLI release workflow](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/.github/workflows/deployment.yml), [uv release workflow](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/main/.github/workflows/release.yml), [Ruff release workflow](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/main/.github/workflows/release.yml), [golangci-lint release workflow](https://github.com/golangci/golangci-lint/blob/main/.github/workflows/release.yml)). Sigstore bundle checks require the exact workflow certificate identity and GitHub OIDC issuer ([cosign blob verification](https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/verifying/verify_blob/), [yq signing workflow](https://github.com/mikefarah/yq/blob/master/.github/workflows/release.yml), [Trivy signing workflow](https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/blob/main/.github/workflows/reusable-release.yaml), [Codex signing action](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/.github/actions/linux-code-sign/action.yml)).

The updater does not check publisher signatures for Go, Rust, abtop, gosec, gitleaks, the ContainerSSH guest agent, tea, kubectl, Helm, Antigravity, OpenCode or the pinned container images. Their checksum, package-manager and digest checks remain. Some of these projects publish signing material; their trust policies need separate review before the updater enforces them. No unsigned-update fallback exists for the publishers in the table.

### Node.js release keyring

The updater takes the newest stable `v26.x.y` from `https://nodejs.org/dist/index.json`. It checks that version's `SHASUMS256.txt.sig` with `gpg` against the keyring in [`scripts/keys/nodejs-release-keys.asc`](../scripts/keys/nodejs-release-keys.asc). A signature from any one of the eight active releasers' keys passes. The updater then reads the two Linux checksums from the verified file.

A failed Node.js check stops the whole scheduled update. `main()` in [`scripts/bump_versions.py`](../scripts/bump_versions.py) returns 1 on any `LookupFailed` and writes no pins, for every tool. This happens when the key that signed the release has expired or been revoked (`EXPKEYSIG` or `REVKEYSIG` in GnuPG's status output, with the message "the pinned signing key needs a hand update") and when a release is signed by a key that is not in the keyring. Updates for all tools resume only after a maintainer refreshes the keyring by hand.

The keyring comes from [`nodejs/release-keys`](https://github.com/nodejs/release-keys/tree/481637f813e912c4aa3622d7964ab426c97b8e8d), at commit `481637f813e912c4aa3622d7964ab426c97b8e8d`. Node.js lists the active releasers in its [release keys section](https://github.com/nodejs/node#release-keys). The scheduled update never changes these files. Refresh the keyring in its own pull request:

1. At the new `nodejs/release-keys` commit, take the fingerprints listed between the `<!-- Active releasers keys -->` markers in its README.
2. Download each `keys/<FINGERPRINT>.asc` at that commit.
3. Import the files into a temporary `GNUPGHOME`.
4. Write `scripts/keys/nodejs-release-keys.asc` with `gpg --armor --export <the fingerprints>`. Do not concatenate the downloaded files. At least one of them has no trailing newline, and plain concatenation silently drops a key.
5. Set `NODE_KEY_FINGERPRINTS` and the commit in its comment in `scripts/bump_versions.py`.
6. Update the commit and the expiry dates in this section.
7. Run the unit tests. `test_node_keyring_holds_exactly_the_pinned_fingerprints` checks the keyring file against the constant.

### AWS CLI signing key

The updater takes the first version heading of the AWS CLI v2 changelog, `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aws/aws-cli/v2/CHANGELOG.rst`, which AWS links as the list of versions ([installing past releases](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-version.html)). For each architecture it downloads `awscli-exe-linux-<x86_64|aarch64>-<version>.zip` and its `.sig` from `https://awscli.amazonaws.com` and checks the signature with `gpg` against [`scripts/keys/aws-cli-public-key.asc`](../scripts/keys/aws-cli-public-key.asc). AWS publishes no checksum for the zips, so the updater computes the SHA-256 pins only after both signatures pass. When the newest version equals `AWSCLI_VERSION`, the updater downloads nothing and keeps the pins.

A failed AWS CLI check stops the whole scheduled update. `main()` returns 1 and writes no pins, for every tool, as for Node.js.

AWS publishes the key as text in the [AWS CLI install guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html), not as a file to download. The file is a copy of that block. The guide lists the key as `AWS CLI Team <aws-cli@amazon.com>`, fingerprint `FB5D B77F D5C1 18B8 0511 ADA8 A631 0ACC 4672 475C`, expiring 2027-07-01. `test_aws_cli_key_holds_exactly_the_pinned_fingerprint` checks the file against `AWSCLI_KEY_FINGERPRINT` in `scripts/bump_versions.py`.

After 2027-07-01, GnuPG reports `EXPKEYSIG` for a release signed with this key, with the message "the pinned signing key needs a hand update". The signature check fails and the scheduled update stops for all tools until a maintainer refreshes `scripts/keys/aws-cli-public-key.asc` from the install guide. To refresh it, copy the key block from the guide into the file, set `AWSCLI_KEY_FINGERPRINT` if the fingerprint changed, update the expiry date here, and run the unit tests.

## Optional extras

`versions.env` pins three npm tools that `agentainer-extras install` adds on request ([Optional extras](extras.md)):

| Pin | npm package | Catalog directory |
|---|---|---|
| `KANDEV_VERSION` | [`kandev`](https://registry.npmjs.org/kandev) | `kandev` |
| `OPENCHAMBER_VERSION` | [`@openchamber/web`](https://registry.npmjs.org/@openchamber/web) | `openchamber` |
| `REA_VERSION` | [`rea-agents`](https://registry.npmjs.org/rea-agents) | `rea` |

Each catalog directory, under `rootfs/usr/local/share/agentainer/extras/`, holds a `package.json` that depends on exactly the pinned version and a `package-lock.json` with an `integrity` hash for every package in the tree. The version in `package.json` must equal the `versions.env` pin, and `tests/host/test-extras-catalog.sh` checks this in CI.

For each extra, [`scripts/bump_versions.py`](../scripts/bump_versions.py):

1. Picks the newest stable, non-deprecated version, no newer than the `latest` dist-tag, whose publish time in the registry's `time` field is at least 7 days old. When that version is not newer than the pin, the pin and the catalog files stay as they are.
2. Regenerates the lockfile with `npm install --package-lock-only --ignore-scripts --before=<now minus 7 days>`, so every dependency in the tree is also at least 7 days old ([npm `before`](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/using-npm/config#before)). It uses an empty npm user config and the public registry.
3. Fails the extra when the new lockfile has a package with an install script (`hasInstallScript`, [package-lock.json](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/configuring-npm/package-lock-json)) that the committed lockfile did not have, unless the package is `node-pty` or `frida`. `agentainer-extras` installs with `--ignore-scripts`, so no install script runs; this check reports a change in the tree for review.
4. Checks every lockfile entry against the registry. The entry must resolve from `https://registry.npmjs.org/`, its `integrity` must equal the registry's `dist.integrity` for that version, and one of the version's `dist.signatures` must verify with `openssl` over `<name>@<version>:<integrity>` with an ECDSA P-256 key in `scripts/keys/npm-registry-keys.json` ([npm registry signatures](https://docs.npmjs.com/about-registry-signatures)). A key with an `expires` time counts only for a version published before that time. A signature by an unknown key does not count. Bundled entries are covered by their parent's integrity; a `link` entry fails.

A failed check for one extra, including a missing `npm` or `openssl`, keeps that extra's pin and catalog files and does not stop the run. The other pins still update. `bump_versions.py --failures FILE` writes one line per failed extra to FILE. In the scheduled workflow, the `extras-failures` job prints those lines in the run summary and fails the run after the pull request for the other pins is open.

The pull request job applies the resolver's patch only when it modifies `versions.env`, `deploy/kubernetes/*/deployment.yaml`, `deploy/kubernetes/agentainer/statefulset.yaml` (the `FILEBROWSER_IMAGE` pin) or an extras `package.json` or `package-lock.json`, and creates, deletes or renames no file ([`.github/actions/bump-pr/action.yml`](../.github/actions/bump-pr/action.yml)).

CI's `lint-unit` job runs `tests/host/test-extras-catalog.sh` and scans the extras lockfiles with Trivy, using the `TRIVY_SCANNER_IMAGE` pin. The scan is report only: findings go to the job's step summary and never fail the job.

## MCP gateway

The image refuses Kelos's own MCP setting, `KELOS_MCP_SERVERS`: Kelos copies header values from a Secret into that variable in plain text, so they would sit in the pod spec. The image reads one MCP server from two files instead, mounted read-only at `/etc/agentainer/mcp` (for example from a Secret with the keys `url` and `token`):

| File | Rule, checked by the guard before any config file is written |
|---|---|
| `url` | One line, at most 512 bytes, matching `^https://[A-Za-z0-9.-]+(:[0-9]{1,5})?(/[A-Za-z0-9._~/-]*)?$` |
| `token` | Matches `^[A-Za-z0-9._~+/=-]{16,4096}$` after one trailing newline is removed |

- The `url` file is the switch. With neither file, no MCP server is configured and the image behaves as before. That includes the empty directory Kubernetes mounts for a missing `optional` Secret.
- With only one of the two files, the pod refuses to start (exit 78).
- A value that breaks its rule is refused with the file's name and never its content. This keeps a quote, backslash, newline or space out of the JSON and TOML that the entrypoints write.
- `AGENTAINER_MCP_TOKEN` set in the pod environment is refused, so the token cannot be put in the pod spec.
- The server is named `gateway`, so Claude's tool names are `mcp__gateway__<tool>`.

Claude: the wrapper writes `~/.claude/mcp-gateway.json` with the URL and `headersHelper` `/usr/local/lib/kelos/mcp-headers`, then passes `--mcp-config` with that file. `--strict-mcp-config` stays, so no other MCP configuration is read. Claude removes credential-like variables from a helper's environment, so the helper reads the token file and prints `{"Authorization":"Bearer <token>"}`. The token is not in the config file, in argv or in claude's environment.

Codex: the entrypoint appends `[mcp_servers.gateway]` with the URL and `bearer_token_env_var = "AGENTAINER_MCP_TOKEN"`, and `[shell_environment_policy.filters]` with `"AGENTAINER_MCP_*" = "exclude"`, after every other write to `config.toml`. It sets `AGENTAINER_MCP_TOKEN` from the file with an assignment prefix on the `codex exec` line, so only that codex process has it. The shell policy removes it from the commands the agent runs.

The agent's shell runs as the same user as the CLI, so it can read the token file, and under Codex the CLI's process environment. These steps keep the token out of the pod spec, argv, the environment of the agent's commands, and the logs. They do not hide it from the agent.

Build: the `kelos-capture` stage of Containerfile.kelos fetches that commit by full SHA (and checks `git rev-parse HEAD` against it), then runs `CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=$TARGETARCH go build -trimpath -ldflags "-X github.com/kelos-dev/kelos/internal/version.Version=v0.62.0-proxy.3" -o /out/kelos-capture ./cmd/kelos-capture` with golang 1.25.14, pinned by index digest in the Containerfile. The fork's go.mod says `go 1.25.0` and has no toolchain line.
